title: Why Africa could back controversial Fifa plan
description: Fifa's plan sell stakes in its competitions to private investors has been heavily criticised, but the body running African football is yet to take a side.
fullText:
In the row which has engulfed global football and the man who runs it, Gianni Infantino, could Africa end up as a lone voice of support for the Fifa president?

While European governing body Uefa has voted to boycott Fifa competitions, including World Cups, if plans go ahead to sell stakes in those competitions to private investors, the Confederation of African Football (Caf) has remained largely silent so far.

Much of that has to do with the close relationship between Caf, Fifa and Infantino.

Caf president Patrice Motsepe lauded Infantino for his "excellent work" after this year's World Cup and hailed the Swiss as "a good friend".

"He is loyal to Africa," Motsepe said on 22 July. "When people have been loyal to you, you never stab them in the back."

Fifa's aim is to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events and allow external investors to buy stakes in it.

Fifa estimates the subsidiary, Fifa Forward Enterprise, could raise $4.2bn (£3.1bn) later this year, with the net benefits being reinvested into the global game.

Caf says its executive committee will meet to "assess and evaluate" the proposal next week, encouraging its member associations to do the same.

African countries have already benefited from previous Fifa funding.

The new sums at stake could continue to transform the footballing landscape on the continent.

Infantino 'wrong man' to lead Fifa says Burnham as criticism grows

Fifa says 'nobody selling football' as plan continues

So far Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs football in North and Central America and the Caribbean, have all opposed Infantino's plan.

But given that many African football federations struggle financially, the lure of $40m (£30m) from Fifa may prove enticing to Caf's 54 member associations, especially as an initial $20m (£15m) could be received as early as 1 January – provided the plans are approved by 19 September.

"Football is a very expensive venture, especially on the African continent where resources are not easy to come by," Rogers Byamukama of Uganda's football federation told the BBC.

"What is wrong with making more money and sharing that money with those that need it most?"

However, Isha Johansen, a former president of the Sierra Leonean FA who also served on Caf's executive committee and the Fifa Council, says the proposal "does not sit well".

"I think people have got to be really realistic here in knowing where we want to see football going in the coming years," she added.

"Should football be commercialised in the manner in which it potentially could be if this proposal were to go through?

"As a businessman or woman you want something out of it. You're not just doing it out of generosity.

"What price does one have to pay in order to get to this elevated development for football in Africa? I think it's going to take a lot of soul-searching [but] I do hope that they (Caf) go along with all the other confederations."

Courting controversy and befriending Trump - the story of Fifa boss Infantino

Caf has developed a close relationship with Fifa since Motsepe and Infantino assumed their respective positions in 2016, with personal as well as business relationships to the fore.

Veron Mosengo-Omba, who served as Motsepe's deputy from 2021 until March this year, was previously chief member associations officer at Fifa - and is a friend of Infantino, having studied law alongside him in Switzerland.

Mosengo-Omba was elected head of DR Congo's football federation in May.

Together he and Motsepe undeniably improved the financial balance sheet at Caf, not least by improving revenues from the Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon), its flagship tournament, while Infantino has done his part to develop the game on the continent.

Africa was the main beneficiary of the expansion of the Fifa World Cup to 48 teams - with the continent awarded a guaranteed nine spots.

The previous allocation, five, had long been seen as a slight in Africa.

"You need to have a president of Fifa who is as committed to African development and growth as Gianni Infantino is," Motsepe said.

"What Gianni has done, to contribute to us increasing the number of African national teams (at the World Cup), [is] enormously important."

A lack of financial resources is a big reason for African member associations - many of whom rely on scant government funding - to back Fifa's proposals.

"Our government cannot manage to give us even $1m (£740,000) every year for football," Malawi FA president Fleetwood Haiya told Newsday on BBC World Service.

"Our government is not able to make sure that they have medical supplies in hospitals [and] at the same time to look at football.

"Malawi needs money. Malawi needs stadiums.

"I'm 100% in support (of the Fifa proposal). There is no dispute. I don't understand why Fifa took so long to do this."

African federations, however, may need to be careful what they wish for, with some people questioning whether governments will continue to fund organisations receiving significant support from elsewhere.

Europe, home to the world's biggest domestic leagues, is undeniably where football is most developed and generates the most commercial income.

The majority of Africa's top footballers play for clubs there, but the argument is their home countries get little in return.

"Uefa is a very rich region," Uganda's Byamukama added.

"But how much of their commercial success has been shared with federations that are poor, for instance in Africa, in Asia?"

Is Infantino finished? Could Uefa boycott World Cup? What happens now?

Is World Cup sell-off plan a step too far by Infantino?

Handily for Fifa and Infantino, African nations who have benefited from Fifa's generosity have been making headlines.

Cape Verde's impressive debut World Cup campaign came after the Blue Sharks upped their spend on logistical arrangements during qualifying.

Haiya says Malawi's performance at the ongoing Women's Africa Cup of Nations, where the Scorchers beat defending champions Nigeria on their debut at the finals, was also built on Fifa funds.

"These girls were not given the opportunity or the platform, or they were not supported to showcase their talents.

"Gianni Infantino believed in our project for women's football."

Byamukama points to money from Fifa helping to fund the construction of Uganda's FA headquarters, a technical centre and a stadium, while a source from another southern African FA said the continent's administrators back Infantino because he has increased financial support.

The promise of more to come would only strengthen that bond.

"It is a good financial comfort for federations in Africa," the official said.

"They can do a lot with grassroots football and infrastructure."

However, Caf's close bond with Fifa has had its downsides, with Motsepe appearing unwilling to challenge Infantino or his organisation's decisions in public.

Fifa was heavily criticised when US authorities refused to allow Somali referee Omar Artan into the country ahead of the World Cup and later also came under fire after suspending a one-match ban handed to United States striker Folarin Balogun for a red card at the tournament.

Caf did not publicly denounce the world governing body on either issue despite scathing statements from elsewhere.

Fifa's expanded Club World Cup, held in June and July last year, meant the 2025 Afcon was forced to move to a December to January slot, causing issues with top European clubs over the release dates for players.

And the decision to hold Afcon every four years from 2028, rather than biennially, was seen as a decision that benefits Fifa and the global football calendar rather than Africa. Fifa general secretary Mattias Grafstrom sat alongside Motsepe when the announcement was made.

Johansen accepts that the funds from Fifa Forward Enterprise would be a game-changer for many in Africa, but she believes the long-term integrity of the game is under threat.

"It is an offer that is hard to refuse," she said.

"We (in Africa) need the money.

"I think we now come to a point where you really need to know where to draw the line and not sacrifice the beautiful game."

Infantino had indicated Fifa's proposals would need a straight majority to go through - meaning 106 of its 211 members need to vote in favour.

Uefa has 55 votes, Asia 46 and Concacaf 35.

Should all member associations from those confederations back the stance of their governing body, that would mean 136 nations are already against Infantino's plan.

Even if Caf's 54 associations do stand behind the Swiss, the weight of the rest of the world could deny the second-largest and second-most populous continent what many view as a welcome windfall.

Additional reporting by BBC Sport Africa's Celestine Karoney.

title: Security plans in place for any Afghanistan protests
description: Cricket Ireland says "appropriate" security plans are "in place" for the forthcoming men's one-day series with Afghanistan amid the possibility of protests.
fullText:
Cricket Ireland says "appropriate" security plans have been drawn up for the forthcoming men's one-day series against Afghanistan amid the possibility of protests.

The governing body has been liaising with stakeholders, including the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI), to ensure the five ODIs pass off without incident.

Cricket Ireland's decision to host the series has been criticised because of the plight of women in Afghanistan who face severe restrictions on their rights and freedoms, with widespread barriers to education, employment, movement, public participation and personal autonomy under Taliban rule.

The first two ODIs will be played in Bready next Wednesday and Friday, with the remaining three fixtures at Stormont on 10, 12 and 15 August.

"Appropriate security measures are in place, and all necessary arrangements have been made to ensure the safety and security of players, supporters, officials and staff," Cricket Ireland told BBC Sport in a statement.

The PSNI said it did "not comment on operational matters" but an "appropriate and proportionate policing plan" will be in place to "ensure the safety of everyone involved" should there be protests at the matches.

"The right to freedom of speech and peaceful assembly are fundamental human rights. They are protected in law and allow individuals to engage in peaceful protest," said a PSNI spokesperson.

"However, these rights are limited by the need to uphold the rights of others, protect public health and safety, minimise disruption to normal life and by the need to prevent and detect crime.

"If the Police Service identifies potential criminal offences, or unacceptable impact on the rights of others, we will take lawful and proportionate action."

Neither England nor Australia schedule bilateral series against Afghanistan, although they fulfil fixtures against them at major international tournaments.

Cricket Ireland chief executive Sarah Keane said shortly after she was appointed earlier this year the decision to host Afghanistan this summer came with some "moral discomfort" given the plight of women in the country.

Female participation in sport has effectively been outlawed since the Tailban returned to power in 2021.

Women have been banned from universities, parks and sports. The Taliban raided the homes of female athletes and many women's cricketers fled Afghanistan for their safety.

Keane was recently appointed to the International Cricket Council's (ICC) special taskforce for the Afghan women's refugee team who are working towards participation in official qualifying events by 2030.

Felix Jakens, a spokesperson for Amnesty International, said the right to protest during the series should be "fully respected by police and organisers alike".

He also called upon Cricket Ireland, its players and the ICC "to be united in speaking out" on the plight of women in Afghanistan.

"As we've seen with other regimes seeking to use sport to launder their image, the Taliban will look to harness this series for propaganda purposes," Jakens told BBC Sport.

"Cricket Ireland and the ICC should ensure that isn't allowed to happen.

"The least they can do is ensure the women and girls of Afghanistan are on the minds of audiences watching, and that this series doesn't become a free propaganda boost for the Taliban."

The Women's Resource & Development Agency, a Belfast-based organisation which seeks to advance women's equality and participation in society, questioned whether the matches should go ahead at all.

"The state of human rights in Afghanistan, and especially the absence of the most fundamental rights of women, should be on everyone's mind as the men's team take on Afghanistan's men's team in cricket," it added in a statement.

"There are legitimate questions as to whether Cricket Ireland should allow such an opportunity to a team which represents a state in which women are second-class citizens at best."

title: Head coach Matos agrees new Swansea contract
description: Swansea City head coach Vitor Matos agrees a new contract that ties him to the Championship club until 2030.
fullText:
Head coach Vitor Matos has agreed a new Swansea City contract which ties him to the Championship club until 2030.

Matos, 38, was appointed on a deal running until 2029 last November.

But Swansea's progress since Matos took charge has convinced the club's hierarchy to hand the Portuguese improved terms.

"From the moment I arrived here, I have sensed how powerful the connection between Swansea City and the fans and community is," said Matos.

"This is something very special, it is a feeling myself and the players love, and the desire to keep building that and sharing great moments together is one of the key motivations in extending my contract with the club."

Chief executive Tom Gorringe said "stability and consistency of vision" were important at what he called an "exciting time for the football club".

"Vitor made a considerable impact following his appointment in November of last year and we are excited about the direction in which he is taking Swansea City," Gorringe added.

"This new deal is a reflection of our belief in the work he and his team have done since joining us, and what we believe we can accomplish together under Vitor's stewardship."

Matos had only brief experience as a manager, at Portuguese club Maritimo, when Swansea turned to him after missing out on Kim Hellberg to Middlesbrough last year.

A former elite development coach at Liverpool – and assistant boss at Red Bull Salzburg – Matos steered Swansea clear of relegation trouble before securing an 11th-placed finish thanks to 14 wins in his 30 league games in charge.

Swansea will begin Matos' first full season in charge with increased expectations based on their improvement last term.

Latest Swansea City news, analysis and fan views

Listen to the latest Swansea City interviews, news and discussion on BBC Sounds

Swans bid farewell to Cullen, a player the coaches loved

Matos has been backed in the transfer market this summer, with Swansea thought to have spent a combined total of about £15m on Moussa Yeo, Elijah Just and Joseph Opoku as well as bringing in defender Stephen Welsh on a free.

There are more signings to come, although Swansea have sold influential midfielder Ethan Galbraith and it remains to be seen whether Zan Vipotnik, last season's Championship top scorer, will still be at the club when the summer transfer window closes.

"We put good foundations in place last season, but now we have to look forward, we have to keep pushing and making progress," Matos added.

"We have enjoyed a positive pre-season, and made good additions to our squad, and I am looking forward to the season ahead and beyond."

Matos' team play their final pre-season friendly at home to Leganes on Saturday before hosting Birmingham City in the Carabao Cup the following weekend.

The new league campaign starts with a trip to Stoke City on Saturday, 15 August.

title: Stokes return would not surprise England chief Key
description: England director of men's cricket Rob Key says he "wouldn't be surprised" if Ben Stokes returns to international cricket, adding that "anything is possible".
fullText:
England director of men's cricket Rob Key says he "wouldn't be surprised" if Ben Stokes came out of international retirement at some stage, adding "anything is possible".

Former captain Stokes, 35, announced his decision to retire from international cricket during England's third Test defeat by New Zealand in June.

Stokes missed the second Test of that 2-1 series loss while an investigation took place into an incident at a London nightclub after he breached the team's midnight curfew.

The all-rounder, who was subsequently found blameless for the incident, said the controversy had "added" to his thoughts about calling time on his illustrious England career.

Brendon McCullum has since been sacked as Test coach and replaced by former New Zealand captain Stephen Fleming, with Joe Root succeeding Stokes as skipper.

Key said the door remains open for Stokes to return for next summer's home Ashes series against Australia - although he has received no indication that Stokes intends to reverse his decision.

"It would be a brilliant story if he does," Key told Sky Sports News. "Anything's possible with Ben."

Former England captain Michael Vaughan believes the appointment of Fleming and Root's return as Test skipper might tempt Stokes to return to the England set-up.

"Root's difficulty will be getting a structure in his team - getting a formula without an all-rounder like Ben Stokes," Vaughan told BBC Sport.

"And I'll keep saying it, I just wonder over the next few months if - I'm sure Ben won't be back in 2026 - but I just wonder if this appointment has given us a little bit of a glimmer that it may happen, that the dream may happen next year, that Ben might come back."

England captaincy could be what Root needs - Vaughan

Fleming new England Test coach with Root captain

Fleming has never previously worked as the head coach of a national team, but led Chennai Super Kings to a record five Indian Premier League (IPL) titles during his 17-year tenure.

Key said England initially narrowed the shortlist for the vacant position down to "three or four different people" - none of whom was Andy Flower - before settling on Fleming.

Former England coach Flower ruled himself out of the running to replace McCullum this month.

According to Key, the appointment of Fleming sets the wheels in motion for England to develop a "world-class team" capable of challenging Australia, and that is able to "sustain" its success.

"English cricket has had periods where we have been really good for a bit and then it falls off," he told BBC Sport.

"We beat the sides below us and we compete against the ones above us.

"We want to create a system to make sure that English cricket not only has success, but sustains it. Fleming will bring all of that."

Root led England in Stokes' absence during the second Test against New Zealand, having previously captained the team from 2017 to 2022.

He made his Test debut in 2012 and holds several England Test records, including being their highest run-scorer on 14,114.

Root is also the second-highest Test run-scorer of all time, behind India legend Sachin Tendulkar, who tops the list with 15,921.

Key said Root was one of several candidates to succeed Stokes as captain and, following Fleming's appointment, it was decided between the pair that the batter was "the best person to do it".

"We spoke to Joe as well and his enthusiasm, the opportunity he feels to continue something that Ben [Stokes] and Brendon [McCullum] had started, to refine it, yes - he's now got one of the most experienced coaches of international players going," said Key.

"He's got one of the best coaches to work with in Stephen Fleming. I can't wait.

"There is nobody who deserves a great period more than Joe Root."

Test Match Special Podcast: Fleming & Root to lead England Test team

Stumped Podcast: New era for England as Fleming appointed Test coach

Although his appointment was confirmed this week, Fleming will not take charge of England's Test series against Pakistan in August.

The 53-year-old will instead be in his native New Zealand with his family before travelling to the United Kingdom next month to begin preparations for England's Test tour of South Africa in December.

Sacking McCullum and the fact Fleming will not begin his role immediately has drawn criticism from some quarters, with suggestions England have wasted a summer of cricket.

However, Key said he "did not agree" with that assessment and believes England have appointed the "best two coaches going".

"You never know what might have happened if we had done it another way," added Key.

England, under McCullum and white-ball captain Harry Brook, recently became the number one ranked T20 side in the world after their 4-0 series win over world champions India.

"That is a new generation, a year and a half into a project with Harry and Brendon," said Key.

"In the Test summer, you never know. We still have plenty of time to come."

title: Celtic reject West Ham Engels bid and confirm Johnston interest
description: Celtic reject a West Ham approach for Arne Engels while there is Everton interest in Alistair Johnston, manager Martin O'Neill confirms.
fullText:
Celtic have rejected a West Ham approach for Arne Engels while Everton are keen on Alistair Johnston, manager Martin O'Neill has confirmed.

The West Ham bid for Belgium midfielder Engels, 22, "doesn't remotely meet our valuation", said O'Neill, who received a call from Everton counterpart David Moyes relating to Canada full-back Johnston, 27.

"Everton have been in contact," explained O'Neill. "I'm not sure whether there's been a bid in there for that one, but they've been in contact saying that there would be.

"In fairness, David Moyes did call me last week to say there would be contact."

Nottingham Forest failed with a February offer worth £25m for Engels, who moved to Celtic Park from Augsburg in August 2024.

Johnston, who started all five of Canada's games at the World Cup, joined the Scottish champions from Montreal in January 2023.

O'Neill described the interest in both players as "disappointing" but "to be expected", adding that it is "difficult to stop people if their ambition is to play in a big, big league".

The 74-year-old went on to say: "Our job is to try and keep them, try and do our best to keep them.

"If that's not possible, naturally we'll have to try and get replacements in. To replace those players would be a difficult task."

Celtic have sold Daizen Maeda to Ipswich Town and brought in forward duo Kasper Hogh and Camilo Duran this summer.

"I felt that something would happen with some of our top players," O'Neill said.

"I was hoping as each day goes past that there wouldn't be any serious interest. But that was never going to happen.

"But we need players in anyway. And we're in the hunt for that. We're getting close. I don't know how close is close, but we are definitely getting close."

title: Why women's football is first casualty of Fifa plans
description: Fifa's president Gianni Infantino's plans will make women's football "the first casualties" according to former England defender Anita Asante.
fullText:
Women's football will be the first to suffer if Fifa president Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in competitions to private investors goes ahead, according to former England defender Anita Asante.

On Thursday European football's 55 member associations voted to boycott all Fifa competitions until the governing body drops Infantino's proposals.

Uefa's stance will first be tested when the Fifa Under-20 Women's World Cup starts on 5 September in Poland.

"The first casualties will be women's football tournaments," Asante told BBC Sport.

"I don't think Fifa have considered the implications of their decision."

The Polish Football Association (PZPN) said on Friday it has not received any information about teams withdrawing from the competition and preparations are continuing as planned.

In October, England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales all have qualifiers for next summer's Women's World Cup in Brazil.

And the Under-17 Women's World Cup is scheduled to take place in October in Morocco.

"That's what's so frustrating for players. You can't take for granted the opportunity to play in the World Cup," said Asante.

"If this isn't resolved by the time of England's qualifiers, then the impact could be huge and it is already a busy schedule."

Infantino 'wrong man' to lead Fifa - Burnham

Fifa says 'nobody selling football' as plan continues

In response to Uefa's boycott, Fifa said on Friday "nobody is selling football" and claimed the consultation process has been "disrupted by incorrect media reports".

Concacaf, which governs football in North and Central America and hosted this year's World Cup, said its 41 member associations have "rejected" Fifa's proposal.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has published a statement saying it "stands in solidarity" with its counterparts in Europe and North, Central America and the Caribbean.

Meanwhile, Carlos Cordeiro, a senior adviser to Fifa chief Gianni Infantino, resigned from his position, saying the proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".

"I was really pleased to see that Uefa had taken the position that they have, and they were very clear with their directive and firm about how they want this to go," added Asante.

"It's taking away what the essence of football is about and tournaments are about. Women could be the casualties here yet again."

Former FA director of women's football Baroness Campbell said it was "tragic" women's football could be first to be impacted.

Speaking to BBC Sport's Jo Currie she said: "I think it's a real shame, but equally, I'm absolutely supportive of them [the regional federations] standing up for what they believe is right for the sport.

"I'm a great believer sport must be pure - it doesn't mean I don't think commercial investment isn't important, it's massively important, but it mustn't take over the game."

Fifa and Infantino want to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, and external investors will be able to buy stakes in it.

It said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).

Infantino has set a deadline of 19 September for football federations to accept his controversial plans.

In a 25-page document created by investment bank JP Morgan, it is made clear Fifa's tournaments would expand to hit an estimated increased pay-out of 24m euros per member association in the 2035-2039 cycle.

It mentions "new business initiatives" and "attracting top talent with incentive-driven compensation".

The World Cup is described in it as the "most widely viewed" sporting event but Fifa, by contrast, is said to be "under-monetised".

There is no mention in the document of the women's game.

If approval is granted, Fifa says Thrive Eternal is expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.

Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.

title: Tour de France Femmes to make history on Ventoux
description: The Tour de France Femmes begins in Lausanne, Switzerland on Saturday, with its first ascent of Mont Ventoux to come.
fullText:
The Tour de France Femmes begins in Lausanne, Switzerland on Saturday - but it's the race's first ascent of the iconic Mont Ventoux that is really exciting fans.

Riders will cover 1,175km across nine stages - the most since the event returned to the World Tour calendar as a stage race in 2022.

That includes the stage-seven slog up one of the most iconic climbs in the sport's history - to the telecommunications and meteorological tower on the top of Provence's Mont Ventoux.

Ventoux has been an iconic mountain stage for the men's Tour for generations, won by legendary figures such as Eddy Merckx, Marco Pantani and Chris Froome.

Alongside in-form rivals such as the Netherlands' Demi Vollering of FDJ-Suez United, last year's winner Pauline Ferrand-Prevot of Visma Lease a Bike will be hoping to steal a march.

"I've climbed Mont Ventoux quite a lot in the past," said the Frenchwoman. "But also since I've known it will be in the Tour de France, I went there quite a few times."

Such trips are useful for Ventoux - a stage that has put paid to many a Tour-winning dream in the past. In 1967, British cyclist Tom Simpson died there.

Ferrand-Prevot will look to repeat her success of last year wearing a jersey designed by children's competition winners.

The idea behind her campaign is to inspire the next generation of cyclists.

Ferrand-Prevot returned to road cycling in 2025 for the Tour and became the first Frenchwoman to win the race since Jeannie Longo in 1989.

Now 34, she initially left road cycling in 2015 to focus on other disciplines in the sport. She competed in mountain biking, cyclo-cross and gravel cycling - winning gold at the Paris Olympics in 2024. She was the first rider to hold all three major discipline world titles simultaneously in 2015.

Ferrand-Prevot excels in all terrain and is the best climber in the peloton, but with the addition of the team time trial this year her rivals will be watching her every move as she hasn't competed in one since 2021.

Vollering also has strong pedigree having won this race in 2023 and come second in 2022, 2024 and 2025.

The Dutch rider has practised her time-trial position in the lead-up to the tour and could pose a real threat to Ferrand-Prevot's chances of going back-to-back.

Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM) is another big rival, having won the Tour by four seconds in 2024 before finishing third in 2025.

The 31-year-old Pole will be banking on her vast experience to give her the edge, after taking to the podium in all four editions of the race.

See all the Tour de France Femmes stages, external

Riding under Niewiadoma-Phinney on the Canyon-SRAM team is Britain's Zoe Backstedt, who is making her Tour debut.

The 21-year-old Welsh rider has an impressive roster of achievements already, with seven wins to her name this season, and a rich family history routed in the Tour.

Her father Magnus won the 19th stage of the 1998 Tour de France.

Backstedt will be aiming for the Tour's stage-four time trial in Dijon, after winning British road race and time-trial titles this year, although her main priority will be supporting the general classification aspirations of her team-mate.

Her sister Elynor (UAE Team L'imad) will also be riding.

Five other Britons start the race.

Picnic-PostNL have three-time British national road race champion Pfeiffer Georgi on their roster giving her team options on the harder transitional stages.

Team-mate Josie Nelson is another British rider capable of turning a hard stage into a result with enough finishing speed to become dangerous when a smaller group reaches the line.

Alice Towers (EF Education-Oatly) was British road champion in 2022, and has strength in the climbs.

Millie Couzens (Fenix-Premier Tech) and Robyn Clay (Picnic-PostNL) complete the starting British riders, mainly on supportive duties.

One notable absentee is 20-year-old Cat Ferguson of Movistar, who misses out on her Tour debut after medical checks revealed two fractures in her ankle.

Justine Ghekiere (AG Insurance–Soudal) and Niewiadoma-Phinney are strong contenders for the polka dot jersey having both won it in previous years. Mavi Garcia (UAE Team L'imad) will be their strongest rival.

Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx-Protime) tops the competitors for the green sprinters' jersey. Elisa Balsamo (Lidl-Trek) and Charlotte Kool (Fenix–Premier Tech) will rival her, with more versatility across different terrains on the course.

Marion Bunel (Visma-Lease a Bike) finished third in the race for the white young riders' jersey in 2024. With the two riders ahead of her now too old to contest for the jersey, she stands a strong chance of winning it.

Julie Bego (Cofidis) and Nienke Vinke (Picnic-PostNL) are also in contention.

title: Rockets beat Super Giants to move into second
description: Half-centuries from Sophia Dunkley and Sophie Luff help Trent Rockets beat Manchester Super Giants by 31 runs and move above their opponents into second in the Hundred table.
fullText:
The Hundred women's competition, Old Trafford

Trent Rockets 153-8 (100 balls): Dunkley 57 (33), Luff 51 (26); Ecclestone 2-24

Manchester Super Giants 122 all out (93 balls): Lanning 35 (24); Gardner 4-16

Half-centuries from Sophia Dunkley and Sophie Luff helped Trent Rockets beat Manchester Super Giants by 31 runs and move above their opponents into second in the Hundred table.

Dunkley hit 57 from 33 balls and Luff 51 from 26 as the pair put on a second-wicket partnership of 91 at Old Trafford, helping set up a score of 153-8.

Ash Gardner then took 4-16 in the Super Giants reply, removing Meg Lanning and Paige Scholfield before returning to take the final two wickets of the match as the home side were bowled out for 122 with seven balls remaining.

Rockets lost Australian opener Beth Mooney for two after being put into bat, but Dunkley and Luff soon put the visitors in control, hitting 14 fours and five sixes between them.

The partnership was broken when Luff was caught by Smriti Mandhana off the bowling off Maitlan Brown, before Sophie Ecclestone removed Dunkley and Bess Heath (0) in the space of three balls.

Rockets lost wickets steadily from that point, their last three dismissals run-outs as they pushed to up their total, with Georgia Adams their third-highest scorer with an unbeaten 20.

Super Giants never got going in their reply, with their best partnership one of 30 between Meg Lanning and Kathryn Bryce (27) for the fifth wicket.

Captain Lanning, who top-scored with 35 from the top of the order, was trapped lbw by Gardner, who had already had Scholfield (3) caught and bowled with her first delivery.

The home side lost their last six wickets for 33 runs with Gardner closing the match with two wickets in three balls, having Ryana MacDonald-Gay caught by Dunkley and then bowling Grace Ballinger.

The four points for Rockets' third win in four games moves them two points above Super Giants, who have two wins, a loss and a no result from their four fixtures.

It's a Hundred double-header on Saturday as Birmingham Phoenix host Welsh Fire and London Spirit play Southern Brave.

The women's and men's fixtures at Edgbaston start at 11:00 and 14:30 BST respectively, while at Lord's the women's tie starts at 14:30 and the men's at 18:00.

title: Flock CEO Admits Flock Alerts on People
description: See how this undercuts the company's years-long 'vehicles only' defense, and the implications inside.
fullText:
Flock has spent years insisting its cameras capture only vehicles, not people: a framing it has deployed in court filings, before city councils, and in public statements as its primary defense against surveillance criticism. The distinction matters to Flock because admitting it tracks people exposes the company to privacy regulation and community cancellations that have already cost it contracts in dozens of cities.

Now, under sustained crisis pressure, CEO Garrett Langley has inadvertently undercut that defense himself. In a LinkedIn post touting the system's daily impact, Langley disclosed that Flock alerted on sex offenders, wanted people, and missing persons and children in a single day: human categories, not vehicle categories.

Cars are not registered as sex offenders. Vehicles are not listed as wanted persons. The moment Flock attaches a human designation to an alert, it has conceded that the system alerts on people.

Flock's "Vehicles Only" Position

Flock's denial that it tracks people is not a casual talking point; it is a repeated, formal, multi-year position stated in its most consequential venues. The record is extensive:

IPVM has previously documented that Flock uses "track" freely when selling to law enforcement and the "vehicle only" qualifier when the audience is the general public. The Norfolk legal filing, in a dispute over the constitutionality of the system, is the starkest version: a formal assertion, in a court proceeding, that the cameras provide no information about any person.

Langley's LinkedIn post cannot be reconciled with that position. The figures he cited: 4,144 sex offenders, 1,687 wanted people, 158 missing persons and children. These are human designations drawn from law enforcement databases. The Flock system generates these alerts by matching a vehicle's license plate against a hotlist tied to a person: a registered sex offender, a subject of an active warrant, a missing individual. The plate is the mechanism; the person is the record.

IPVM supports finding missing children and apprehending wanted criminals. Flock could honestly argue that alerting on people (sex offenders, wanted persons, missing individuals) is exactly the point, and that the societal benefit justifies it. That would be a defensible position. What is not honest is simultaneously claiming, as Flock's own website does, that its cameras collect "nothing tied to individuals" and are "not used for watching people."

As the Institute for Justice stated in January 2025:

Langley's LinkedIn post is a more public version of the same slip his own chief legal officer made on a live broadcast. As IPVM reported in May 2026, CLO Dan Haley, during a broadcast in which he was defending Flock's vehicle-only position, accidentally said the system "points to a person, or a vehicle, rather," correcting himself three times in two seconds. The correction was telling: Haley knew the official line, reached for the natural description, and had to stop himself.

Langley did not stop himself. Under pressure to demonstrate the system's value, he posted human-category figures publicly on LinkedIn. The CLO slipped accidentally; the CEO did it deliberately. The result is the same: Flock's own executives, in their most candid moments, describe a system that alerts on people.

Flock has built two incompatible messages: human outcomes for law enforcement and investors, vehicle-only framing for courts and city councils. The CEO has now publicly stated both. Flock needs to pick one. If the system alerts on sex offenders, wanted people, and missing children, it tracks people. If it only captures vehicles with no information about any person, it cannot credibly claim those human-category outcomes. The contradiction is now Langley's own.

title: Newcastle confirm Howe resignation as head coach
description: Eddie Howe steps down as head coach of Newcastle United after nearly five years in charge.
fullText:
Eddie Howe has stepped down as head coach of Newcastle United.

The 48-year-old has left after nearly five years in charge, following a disappointing season in which the Magpies finished 12th in the Premier League.

Howe helped Newcastle earn Champions League qualification on two occasions, and win the Carabao Cup in 2024-25 - their first domestic trophy in 70 years.

"After a period of personal reflection, I have decided that now is the right time for me to step away from my role," said Howe.

Newcastle said the process to recruit a new head coach is at an advanced stage. German coach Matthias Jaissle is favourite to be given the position.

Challenging times ahead for Newcastle - Shearer

Howe going as spending rules bite - troubles for Newcastle's Saudi owners

The winner who played for Tuchel - potential Newcastle boss Jaissle

Howe added: "After nearly five years of giving my life, heart and soul into the club with unrelenting energy, I feel that it is in the best interests of both myself and the club to step away, recharge and take a break.

"Although it's been incredibly difficult to make this decision, I know in my heart that it's the right one.

"It has been the privilege of my lifetime to have been the manager of Newcastle United."

Howe's coaches Jason Tindall, Graeme Jones, Stephen Purches and Simon Weatherstone will also leave St James' Park, as well as head of performance Dan Hodges.

Howe took charge in November 2021 and steered the Magpies to an 11th-place finish that season.

In 2022-23 they qualified for the Champions League and did so again in 2024-25, as well as winning the League Cup.

Last season they reached the Champions League knockout phase for the first time, losing to Barcelona in the last 16, but lost 17 of their 38 Premier League games and failed to secure European football next season.

"There have been so many incredible moments in our time here," Howe added. "From fighting relegation in our first season to the numerous unforgettable nights at St James' Park in the Champions League soon after. The progression was fast.

"Everyone came together, united and what a force we became. These are all memories that I will cherish for the rest of my life."

Howe's final match in charge was a 4-1 defeat by Bristol City at Ashton Gate in a pre-season friendly on Wednesday.

The Magpies have lost two key midfielders this summer - Sandro Tonali to Tottenham and Anthony Gordon to Barcelona, while Arsenal are chasing captain Bruno Guimaraes, who has made it clear he wants to join the Premier League champions.

Last summer, Newcastle spent in the region of £240m on new players, but Howe was left frustrated when Alexander Isak's drawn-out transfer saga ended with the Sweden striker joining Liverpool for a British record of £125m.

"I remain incredibly positive and enthusiastic about the future of Newcastle," said Howe.

"The club is in fantastic hands with a great leadership team and I have no doubt together, alongside whoever comes in to replace me, they will continue to deliver success on the pitch."

Newcastle's chief executive David Hopkinson added: "Eddie and his staff leave with the deep gratitude and respect of everyone at Newcastle United, and with a lasting place in the club's history.

"While we are naturally disappointed to see Eddie leave, we remain immensely thankful for everything he has done for the club."

title: Chelsea's Mudryk free to play after appeal against doping ban
description: Chelsea and Ukraine winger Mykhailo Mudryk has not played since November 2024, and has been unable to access the club's training ground.
fullText:
Chelsea winger Mykhailo Mudryk is available to return to playing immediately after resolving his doping case with the Football Association.

The Ukraine international, 25, has not played a competitive match since November 2024, having been provisionally suspended after returning an "adverse finding" for banned substance meldonium.

He was subsequently given the maximum four-year ban by the FA but appealed against the decision to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas).

The FA said anti-doping disciplinary proceedings have now been resolved with Mudryk and he can return to competition "with immediate effect" after he accepted breaking anti-doping rules and agreed to a suspension equal to the time already served.

Mudryk said he was "grateful" to able to return to playing after "the most difficult period" of his career.

He added: "As I have always maintained from the outset of this case, I have never knowingly or intentionally taken any banned substance."

Chelsea said they are looking forward to helping Mudyk "return to full fitness, back into the squad and back onto the pitch" and he will join the club's pre-season tour.

Mudryk said he expresses "deep gratitude" to everyone at Chelsea and is looking forward to the "next chapter" of his career.

Chelsea fined but avoid suspended points deduction

The FA never previously disclosed details of the case, because their anti-doping programme is deemed strictly confidential.

However, their statement on Friday confirmed Mudryk returned an adverse finding for meldonium, which can increase respiratory capacity and stamina, in an out-of-competition test on international duty with Ukraine in October 2024.

He was charged by the FA in June 2025 and given a four-year suspension in January, which came to light in April after he appealed against the ban to Cas.

The FA said the test showed "a low concentration" of the prohibited cardiovascular medication.

It added that changes have since been made to the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada) technical document regarding meldonium.

The FA said the changes are "not retroactive" but noted that had Mudryk's test been conducted today then "the concentration of meldonium in the sample would not have been reported" and no adverse finding would have been recorded.

In a separate case resolution agreement to his Cas appeal, Mudryk and the FA have now, with the agreement of Wada, resolved the proceedings, leaving him able to return to all forms of competition.

Mudryk remains contracted with Chelsea until 2031, having signed a long deal when he joined for £61m from Shakhtar Donetsk in 2022, as part of the club's plan to amortise the cost of transfers and contracts.

Amortisation means spreading costs out over many years in order to reduce them in each year of a business' accounts.

Had Mudryk's four-year ban remained in place, he would have been unable to play again until roughly December 2028.

Chelsea said the club are "pleased that the matter has now reached a conclusion which allows him to return to football with immediate effect".

They added: "We have always supported Misha throughout this process while fully respecting the integrity of the anti-doping system and the legal process."

The Blues also drew attention to advances in testing that mean "no anti-doping rule violation would have resulted" from Mudryk's sample under current guidelines, saying it is "an important part of the context surrounding the agreed resolution and allows everyone involved to move forward".

Sources close to Mudryk say he is confident of returning to his best form, citing the work he has put in to maintain his fitness during 20 months on the sidelines.

They also point to the support Chelsea have provided throughout the process, while adhering to the restrictions imposed by his suspension and respecting the legal proceedings.

The Ukrainian received backing from the club from afar, while also being given the space to navigate what those close to him describe as an extremely difficult period.

Under the terms of the suspension, Mudryk was unable to access Chelsea's training ground or work with club staff. His only known public interaction with members of the first-team squad came at the Conference League final celebrations in May 2025.

To maintain his fitness, Mudryk paid for private coaching and hired goalkeepers for individual sessions while using a pitch at non-league club Uxbridge FC in London. He also organised a training camp in Austria, with videos from those sessions showing him scoring goals and taking part in attacking drills.

However, those close to Mudryk acknowledge there is no substitute for training and competing alongside elite players on a daily basis. Mudryk is understood to be realistic about the challenge ahead, but believes he can overcome it.

Chelsea are prepared to provide a pathway back into professional football. Whether that involves reintegration into the first team, a loan move - potentially involving sister club Strasbourg - or a permanent transfer remains to be seen.

Whatever the outcome, the resolution of the case represents a significant moment for Mudryk. He now has the opportunity to resume his career and determine what the next chapter looks like.

Having joined Chelsea in one of the most closely watched transfer sagas of 2023, his story at Stamford Bridge is not over yet.

title: 'At least I'll sleep well tonight' - Fifa executive joins Burnham in questioning Infantino
description: Fifa's chief operating officer strongly criticises Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in competitions to private investors.
fullText:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino's position came under further scrutiny on Friday as the governing body's chief operating officer strongly criticised his plan to sell stakes in competitions to private investors.

In a statement released to the Associated Press, Kevin Lamour described the controversial plans as "the project of one person" and said "the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions".

He added Fifa's own administration was "deceived" about the project. BBC Sport has approached Fifa for comment.

The lengthy statement did not mention Infantino by name.

It came on the same day a third confederation spoke out against the plans, a senior adviser to Infantino resigned, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the Swiss was "the wrong man" to lead Fifa.

US President Donald Trump - addressing the proposals for the first time - said he had not spoken to Infantino about the plans.

The two have developed a close relationship since Trump assumed office for a second time in 2025.

Lamour said in his statement: "Our mission - the mission of the hundreds of passionate, dedicated, and exemplary Fifa employees - is to serve football.

"A president must bring people together, unite them, and inspire them. Today, we are experiencing the opposite."

Lamour acknowledged he had a duty of loyalty to his employer but also to "certain values" and supporting his colleagues.

"If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he added. "I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

Fifa says 'nobody selling football' as plan continues

Courting controversy and befriending Trump - the story of Fifa boss Infantino

Why women's football is first casualty of Fifa plans

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) had earlier said it "stands in solidarity" with counterparts in Europe and North, Central America and the Caribbean.

The AFC added Infantino's plan could not "realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward".

"The Fifa World Cup is the pinnacle of global football and derives its strength from the participation of all Confederations and the world's leading football nations," it said.

"Any proposal that risks undermining the unity and universal character of the competition must be reconsidered."

Shortly after that statement, Carlos Cordeiro - Infantino's senior adviser on global strategy and governance - resigned, saying the proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".

Burnham later described Infantino's proposal as an "outrageous suggestion".

"The idea that it could even be brought forward shows that, in my view, [he] is the wrong man to lead the organisation," he added.

The AFC's statement means Infantino's plans are unlikely to be approved by Fifa members if put to a vote.

Infantino had indicated the proposals would need a straight majority to go through - meaning 106 of its 211 members needed to vote in favour for the proposal.

Uefa - the body that governs European football - has 55 votes. Concacaf, which oversees football in North, Central America and the Caribbean, has 35 and Asia has 46.

Should all member associations back the stance of their governing body, that would mean 136 nations are against Infantino's plan.

Fifa and Infantino want to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, and external investors will be able to buy stakes in it.

It said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).

In a 25-page document created by investment bank JP Morgan, it is made clear Fifa's tournaments would expand to hit an estimated increased pay-out of 24m euros per member association in the 2035-2039 cycle.

It mentions "new business initiatives" and "attracting top talent with incentive-driven compensation".

The World Cup is described in it as the "most widely viewed" sporting event but Fifa, by contrast, is said to be "under-monetised".

There is no mention in the document of the women's game.

If approval is granted, Fifa says Thrive Eternal is expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.

Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.

As chief operating officer, Lamour is two layers of management below Infantino.

In his statement - which has been seen by BBC Sport - Lamour said "what has been announced in recent days and what has been happening behind the scenes in recent months defies belief and imagination".

"It is becoming increasingly difficult for Fifa's administration to work under these conditions and fulfil its mission," he wrote.

"I have no authority to speak on behalf of my colleagues, and perhaps I am mistaken. But my feeling is that we all want to be proud to work for Fifa, and today, unfortunately, it seems that is no longer the case for many of us.

"I know I have a duty of loyalty to my employer. But I also, and above all, have a duty of loyalty to certain values and to support my colleagues."

Lamour joined Fifa in November 2024, having previously served as deputy general secretary at Uefa.

Cordeiro, meanwhile, had been a Fifa senior adviser for four years and 11 months.

He represented the world governing body on the White House taskforce for the 2026 World Cup and was a former investment banker with Goldman Sachs.

Appointed in September 2021, he is the first senior figure at Fifa to resign over the plans.

In a lengthy statement, Cordeiro said he "unequivocally" opposed the plans and said he "did not accept the proposition" Fifa needed outside investors to "unlock greater value".

"The proposal has become a defining question for Fifa's future," he wrote.

"Fifa's responsibility is not to maximise commercial returns at any cost. It is to protect and strengthen football for future generations.

"When those principles come into conflict, football must come first."

Cordeiro said he had no involvement in this proposal.

"Most troubling of all is the absence of answers to fundamental questions," he added. "Why this deal? Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits?" he wrote.

"These questions remain largely unanswered, and yet member associations are being asked to make a decision of enormous consequence in barely 50 days or risk being left behind.

"That is not a responsible way to determine the future of the world's game."

The AFC in their statement accused Fifa of setting the "direction of travel" for a "significant initiative" before consulting stakeholders.

It said Fifa's failure to consult its member associations on the proposals had "exposed fundamental weaknesses in Fifa's consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed".

The AFC also criticised Fifa for leaving "confederations, member associations and even Fifa's own governing bodies, including the Fifa Council, feeling sidelined."

It added: "The Fifa World Cup, and the game itself, belong to the entire global football family.

"Their future must always be shaped collectively, through institutions that reflect the voices of all Confederations and member associations.

"The AFC calls upon Fifa to undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework to ensure that proposals of global significance are developed through proper consultation, meaningful engagement and appropriate oversight by Fifa's statutory bodies."

Uefa to boycott World Cups if Fifa plans approved

On Thursday, Uefa voted to boycott World Cups if the Fifa plan proceeded.

Hours later, Concacaf, which hosted this year's World Cup, released a statement also rejecting the proposals made by Infantino.

Fifa released a statement early on Friday vowing to continue with the plan - but added "nobody is selling football".

The governing body of world football claimed the consultation process had been "disrupted by incorrect media reports".

It claimed that would "not come at the cost of either the spirit or the governance of Fifa or football itself".

Uefa has accused Fifa of using football "to enrich themselves and their friends", while Concacaf and AFC have both expressed concerns about consultation over the plans.

"The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product," Uefa's statement on Thursday read.

"It is one of football's greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent.

"No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.

The governing body overseeing football in South America, Conmebol, is yet to publicly comment on the proposals. The governing bodies in Africa (CAF) and Oceania (OFC) have said they will discuss Fifa's plan in August.

While Uefa members are among the richest on the planet, many other nations rely on Fifa funding for basic infrastructure.

While the AFC opposes Infantino's plan, unlike Uefa it has not threatened to boycott Fifa competitions. AFC members would not be obliged to vote against the proposals.

Rogers Byamukama, of the Ugandan Football Federation, argued any avenue that could lead to more resources for nations like his should be explored.

"First and foremost, you need to understand that football is a very expensive venture, especially on the African continent where the resources are not easy to come by," he told Newsday on BBC World Service.

"For instance in Uganda, the number of infrastructure projects that have been funded by Fifa from the resources generated by Fifa, especially at the World Cup, both from ticket sales as well as sponsors.

"On top of that, there are many grassroots programmes that have been funded by Fifa, including schools for football.

"From my perspective, any avenue that brings in more resources is good because those resources would be distributed and given to federations, especially on the African continent and that would inspire growth."

Byamukama acknowledged Uefa's right to speak out, but suggested its members were not reliant on Fifa funding like many associations in the rest of the world where Infantino remains popular.

In the first two cycles of the Fifa Forward development programme, through to 2022, $2.8bn (£2.08bn) was made available for investment across the 211 member associations.

Fifa Forward 3.0 - covering the years 2023 through to 2026 - has produced a 30% increase in funding.

Fifa has provided a further $5m (£3.7m) for every member association, with another $60m (£44.48m) paid to each confederation for their own projects.

After expanding the men's World Cup to 48 teams from 32 for the 2026 edition, Fifa is seeking an independent agency to assess an expansion to 64 teams for the 2030 tournament.

The timeline on documents seen by BBC Sport said Fifa would receive agency proposals by 7 August, with a Fifa decision on 14 August. Delivery of analysis by the agency is then scheduled for 11 September.
