title: MLB trade deadline: Latest rumors on Tarik Skubal, Hunter Greene, and more
description: What are the latest rumors ahead of the MLB Trade Deadline?
fullText:
If you believe Jeff Passan, today is the day we will start seeing trades ahead of the MLB Trade Deadline, which arrives Monday.

So let’s spin around the rumors again.

Wednesday afternoon, Tarik Skubal exited the Detroit Tigers’ game against the Baltimore Orioles in the top of the seventh, having given up a two-run single. He left to a standing ovation from the Detroit faithful, who were wondering like the rest of us whether it was his last outing for the Tigers. He exited having handed the Detroit bullpen a 7-1 lead with two outs and a pair of runners aboard.

What happened after that is, according to one MLB executive, the final “sign” that the Tigers need to move their ace at the deadline.

Baltimore scored four more runs in the inning, and went on to win 10-9 in extras. Despite recording his 1,000th strikeout in the performance, Skubal received a no-decision for his efforts.

“If there was ever a sign that the Tigers should trade Skubal, that was it. The offers should start flowing in any minute,” said one NL executive to MLB insider Mark Feinsand.

Feinsand was not the only one reporting that a deal would be happening. ESPN’s Jeff Passan declared Skubal “will be traded” in his MLB Trade Deadline preview as well.

So what teams could be making a move for the ace? As we outlined yesterday the Milwaukee Brewers are among the suitors, and Patrick Mooney of The Athletic reported that the Chicago Cubs are expected to make a run at the left-hander. But according to Passan, when it comes to potential suitors they are “all almost resigned to the idea that the Los Angeles Dodgers are going to get Tarik Skubal.”

A potential reason for that? The lingering health issues for Shohei Ohtani. With the superstar dealing with left knee and right bicep issues, it has put his time on the bump on hold. His last start came on July 3, and manager Dave Roberts indicated earlier this week that his throwing program is on hold. “Trying to mitigate that, we stopped the throwing, stopped the bullpens — hopefully, No. 1, take care of the knee and then not have him try to create velocity with the arm that’s not 100%,” Roberts said.

With Ohtani on the shelf — as a pitcher — that could mean a big push for Skubal from the Dodgers.

If you’re looking for a sleeper team in the Skubal sweepstakes, keep an eye on Tampa Bay. The Rays saw left-hander Shane McClanahan leave his start on Thursday with “back tightness,” and while it is not considered a “long-term” issue, there is an opening for Tampa Bay. As one MLB source told MLB.com, “[t]he Brewers, Rays and Dodgers have the most high-end prospects to move. It would be somewhat surprising if he didn’t wind up with one of those three teams.”

While Skubal will command the headlines, another top arm could be on the move.

According to MLB.com, there is a “50-50” chance that the Cincinnati Reds move flame-thrower Hunter Greene ahead of the MLB Trade Deadline. Greene missed the first half of the season following surgery to remove bone chips from his right elbow, as he put off the surgery last season and threw through the discomfort, option for an injection rather than surgery.

He ultimately went under the knife in the spring, costing him the start to 2026. Since returning he has gone 2-2 with a 7.06 ERA in four starts this season.

But this is a former All-Star, who is under club control for the next few seasons. He signed a six-year extension with Cincinnati in 2023, and is controlled through 2028. Greene is owed $15 million in 2027, $16 million in 2028, and has a $21 million club option for 2029, and his contract comes with a $2 million buyout.

His health is probably the biggest concern, as he has missed time beyond the recent surgery. Tommy John surgery in 2018 cost him the entire 2019 Minor League campaign, and he has lost time due to shoulder and lower-body issues.

“Health,” said one MLB executive to MLB.com about the concern. “He falls into the high quality and moderate-to-low quantity category.”

Still, during his 2024 All-Star campaign, he went 9-5 with a 2.75 ERA, earning Cy Young votes. Teams that miss on Skubal could be enticed to bet on that talent — at that low cost — for the next few years.

Our friends at Battery Power are taking about Greene as well:

As we noted yesterday, the New York Yankees are one of several teams looking for help behind the plate at the MLB Trade Deadline.

According to longtime MLB insider Jon Heyman, the Yankees have inquired with the Baltimore Orioles about Adley Rutschman, but from the outside looking in it would seem unlikely that Mike Elias would move the catcher within the division:

Yankees are among many teams to check on 3-time All-Star/switch-hitting catcher Adley Rutschman. NYY is casting a wide net for catching need. Ryan Jeffers, pending free agent, seemed logical but Twins suggest they’re a buyer now. Tyler Stephenson, others are on NYY list

— Jon Heyman (@JonHeyman) July 29, 2026

However, Passan reported on his podcast earlier this week that the Orioles are at least “open” to moving players such as Rutschman. Open is one thing, but making a deal … and one to the Yankees … is another.

Colorado Rockies catcher Hunter Goodman is another option generating buzz, given last year’s slash line of .278/.323/.520, but the fact that he has three arbitration years coming up before he becomes a free agent in 2030 has pushed the asking price up.

With the Los Angeles Dodgers running away with things in the NL West, the San Diego Padres sit in third place, 14 games back in the division.

But at one game over .500, the Padres are just two games out in the NL Wild Card chase, so moving a key player ahead of hte deadline does not seem likely.

Until you remember general manager A.J. Preller is involved

After swinging last year’s biggest move, the deal with the Athletics for closer Mason Miller, could Preller really turn around and trade him at the 2026 MLB Trade Deadline? According to Passan it is at least possible, but Preller has been telling teams that no prospect can be listed as off limits in such a deal.

With the New York Mets mired at the bottom of the NL standings, they are expected to move some players ahead of the deadline.

One of them could be right-hander Clay Holmes.

Holmes has not pitched in the majors since mid-May, when he suffered a broken right fibula, but was 4-4 in his nine starts with a 2.39 ERA and WHIP of 1.101. He pitched four scoreless innings for Low-A St. Lucia earlier this week, a game that was attended by scouts from several teams including the Yankees, White Sox, Phillies, Rays, Rangers, Dodgers, according to The Athletic.

He is set to hit free agency at the end of the season, but is still expected to have a “strong” market. One AL executive told FanSided that “[i]t would be a surprise if he didn’t [get traded].”

title: Joe Root’s return as Test captain highlights English cricket’s missing generation
description: Root has been reappointed after Ben Stokes’s retirement with Harry Brook overlooked – but where are England’s other Test leaders?
fullText:
Amid recent reflection on the so-called “summer of four captains” of 1988, the witticism around English cricket has been that at least, then, they had four options from which to choose. As Rob Key worked through the process of appointing a new Test head coach, he spoke to each of the candidates about who they would want as captain were they to get the job. It would be a surprise if more than two names were realistically mentioned; a binary choice, it seems, between Harry Brook and Joe Root led to Key and Stephen Fleming agreeing that it was “too soon” for the former’s elevation.

Welcome back, then, to a skipper who has won one of his last 18 Tests in charge; an individual so worn down by the role last time that he described developing an “unhealthy relationship” with the captaincy. Say it ain’t Joe? It is to Root’s credit that, when asked to wear the blazer again, there was no hesitation in accepting – but it is hard to shake a sense that an offer to a 35-year-old who had already led his country in a record 65 matches would not, in an ideal world, have been forthcoming.

Key, as is custom, saw the positives. “He is our best ever batter, and now has the chance to captain the side without any of the stuff he had to deal with last time,” England’s managing director of men’s cricket said of Root, with reference to the dark, Covid-confused days at the end of his first tenure. “I’m just so glad he gets that chance.” A second innings as Test skipper is a rarity; England must hope Root is more Mike Brearley than David Gower.

That he had to be reappointed (and it is probably fair to describe it in those terms) suggests a dereliction of duty in succession planning. Key made passing reference to the sudden but perhaps not entirely surprising retirement of Ben Stokes as he sought to explain his decision-making, suggesting that the need for a new Test skipper had perhaps come sooner than he and the rest of the ECB hierarchy had planned.

There are threads to be pulled at within that, though. The first, of course, concerns Brook, regarded widely – and as opposed to common misconception – as a natural leader and intuitive cricketing thinker, and clearly groomed as the Test captain of the future. And yet to hear Key suggest that it was “too soon” for a man installed as Stokes’ deputy ahead of the Ashes, and one that has led England in white-ball cricket for more than a year, rather jarred. Clearly, the busy schedule played a part – it is surely impossible to straddle all three formats as skipper – but at a time where a new identity must be forged, there is a sense that an opportunity to set that more directly has been missed.

Alternately, one might ponder where the rest of England’s captaincy candidates are – or even where they are coming from. There is a striking lack of seniority within the current set-up, as highlighted by the callow unit that took the field at the Oval when Stokes was stood down during the New Zealand series. Even accounting for Ben Duckett, a three-format cricketer who England have not appeared keen to promote into any kind of leadership capacity, there would seem no-one with both clout and comfort within the environment. Were Root and Brook, his presumed deputy, to each go down on the eve of a Test, it might have to be Jacob Bethell to step in.

“It needs to be worked on, but it is very hard to put you on a course to become England captain,” Key conceded. “It is unfortunate, I think, with Ollie Pope and Zak Crawley – Ollie had been vice-captain and Zak a senior player.” England were desperate for one or t’other to really seize their spot; that neither could, despite tremendous patience, has exacerbated matters. “The shame is that their form got in the way of them being able to stay in the side. Then that void wouldn’t have been there as much. We would have had two outstanding leaders.” Others may look at recent County Championship-winning skippers in Rory Burns and Haseeb Hameed, who have each flourished as leaders after their time with England had come and gone.

“I think [Crawley and Pope] can both come again,” it was stressed. “But clearly there is a gap between Harry Brook and the people younger than him like Jacob Bethell, who we are trying to bring in. All of this happened a little bit too soon, probably.” Out of that summer of 1988 came the fast-tracking of three future England captains – perhaps Brook, Jacob Bethell and Jamie Smith, all skippers at U19 level, may yet emerge as the Michael Atherton, Nasser Hussain and Alec Stewart of the modern-day.

But England have felt caught between a generation on the wane and one yet to fully emerge. Within white-ball cricket, with the many opportunities that the franchise system provides, there is a growing group of English players in their prime developing captaincy experience, but those same chances in red-ball cricket are limited – in part because of the lure of overseas leagues. Of the 18 first-class county captains, only really Ollie Robinson could currently be termed a realistic England Test inclusion – and an elevation to the national captaincy will not be forthcoming for a variety of reasons.

There was a sense of wistfulness over the senior heads lost, for a variety of reasons, in the last few years: Jonny Bairstow, James Anderson, Stuart Broad, Chris Woakes, Moeen Ali, now Stokes. It was revitalising that group that proved the great success of the early McCullum era; now the challenge is altogether different.

“I feel like we’ve lost a whole generation of cricketer, and we’ve only got Joe Root left,” Key said, without direct reference to anyone in particular. “Four years ago, I felt we needed to change the mentality of English cricket. Ben and Brendon did that brilliantly. In Stephen and Joe, I think we’ve got the two best people to take a side with a huge amount of potential who need refinement.”

title: NI striker Marshall makes Luton switch from West Ham
description: West Ham United and Northern Ireland striker Callum Marshall joins League One club Luton Town for an undisclosed fee.
fullText:
West Ham United and Northern Ireland striker Callum Marshall has joined League One club Luton Town for an undisclosed fee.

Luton said the 21-year-old has agreed a "long-term" contract.

Marshall made three first-team appearances for West Ham after signing from Linfield in January 2022 and was part of the squad that won the FA Youth Cup in 2023.

He spent the 2024-25 season playing in League One for Huddersfield Town, scoring 10 goals during a loan spell, and ended last season in Germany on loan at Bochum.

Luton boss Jack Wilshere told the club website:, external "From the first moment I met Callum, I knew how hungry he was for success.

"Naturally, a lot of other clubs were in for him, so we're pleased that he's chosen us and that we're a club that's matching his ambition and vice-versa."

Marshall said he felt the move is a "great next step for my career" and Luton is a club "heading in the right direction".

title: England prospect Perrin 'has the shots' on return
description: England prospect Davina Perrin says she remembers she has "got the shots" after recovering from injury.
fullText:
England prospect Davina Perrin said she remembered she has "got the shots" after recovering from injury.

The 19-year-old was touted for England recognition last season after hammering the fastest century in the history of the women's Hundred, a 43-ball 101 for Northern Superchargers in the eliminator match.

She struck 52 from 43 deliveries in Birmingham Phoenix's 24-run defeat by Southern Brave on Thursday, her second match back after a month on the sidelines.

"It's my first like proper injury so there's so much learnings from it and that's the big thing for me, looking at what I can learn from the experience," said Perrin.

"Seeking advice where I could as well - I managed to grab a few minutes out of [former England wicketkeeper] Sarah Taylor and she gave me a really good bit of advice.

"I wasn't feeling great and she just said 'don't try and be the player that you were before, be the player that you are now' and that really stuck with me - a reminder to be fearless, you've got the shots. That definitely helped today."

Perrin was signed by Big Bash League franchise Melbourne Renegades last season, but was dismissed for a golden duck on debut and averaged 9.60 from five matches.

She was the first player drawn at the inaugural Hundred auction in March, joining Phoenix for £50,000 having played the previous two seasons for Superchargers.

After averaging 40.50 in seven matches in this season's One-Day Cup for Warwickshire, her injury issues meant she was only able to feature in one T20 Blast fixture.

She was dropped three times by Brave in Thursday's innings before she was caught by Maia Bouchier off the bowling of Sarah Glenn, and Perrin said she uses her 2025 century to boost her confidence.

"I think for me it was remembering you utilise that as a token of what you can do and what you're capable of," Perrin added.

"Doesn't mean I'm going to do it every day, you fail more than you succeed in cricket. When you have an innings like that behind you, it's also a nice gentle reminder that you're not awful at cricket.

"It's a sign of my ceiling and I'd love to like exceed that someday."

title: Boulter to lead GB at Billie Jean King Cup finals
description: Katie Boulter will lead the British team competing at the Billie Jean Cup finals in Shenzen, China, in September.
fullText:
Katie Boulter will lead the British team at the Billie Jean Cup Finals in Shenzhen, China.

Emma Raducanu, who has struggled with injury and illness throughout the year, has not been named in the squad.

British number two Boulter replaces Katie Swan in a team that is otherwise unchanged from their qualifying win against Australia, in Harriet Dart, Mika Stojsavljevic and Jodie Burrage.

Britain begin their campaign against the Czech Republic on Tuesday, 22 September.

In April, 17-year-old Stojsavljevic starred with a singles win over world number 56 Talia Gibson as Britain upset the home side in Melbourne to qualify for their fourth finals in five years.

"I'm pleased to select Katie Boulter, who knows what it's like to step up on occasions like this, and the three women who played with so much heart and courage to upset Australia earlier this year," said Great Britain captain Anne Keothavong.

"Czechia will be a very challenging first match for us but the players and I believe in our chances, since we have a very strong record in recent finals."

Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova and runner-up Karolina Muchova are in the team for 11-time winners Czechia, who Britain face in the quarter-finals.

World number two Elena Rybakina will lead Kazakhstan, who play Spain, while Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen leads hosts China as they challenge defending champions Italy, featuring Olympic doubles gold pair Jasmine Paolini and Sara Errani.

Ukraine and Belgium complete the last-eight line-up, with all ties at the finals to be decided in a best-of-three format of two singles and one doubles.

title: Liverpool's Jones argues with Szoboszlai after game
description: Liverpool's Curtis Jones has a heated argument with team-mate Dominik Szoboszlai after his side's win over Wrexham.
fullText:
Liverpool midfielder Curtis Jones had a heated argument with team-mate Dominik Szoboszlai after his side's 1-0 win over Wrexham at Yankee Stadium on Thursday.

After the full-time whistle Jones, Szoboszlai and later Kostas Tsimikas argued with one another as the team were walking across the pitch to applaud supporters.

It is unclear what caused the exchange although during the match Szoboszlai gave his captain's armband to Tsimikas rather than Jones when he was subbed off and during the argument Tsimikas was filmed throwing the armband on to the floor.

Earlier this summer Liverpool rejected a £21.7m offer for Jones from Inter Milan.

The 25-year-old has one year left on his current deal at Anfield.

Earlier this month Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola stressed he wanted Jones to stay at the club.

"I rate Curtis very highly," he said. "For me he is a great, great player, and I hope he can continue with us and continue performing the way he has been performing."

Liverpool finish their pre-season tour of North America on Sunday (21:00 BST) when they face Leeds in Chicago.

title: Venner and Robinson among 32 Red Roses contracts
description: Gloucester-Hartpury wing Mia Venner and Exeter scrum-half Flo Robinson receive full-time England contracts for the first time.
fullText:
Gloucester-Hartpury wing Mia Venner and Exeter scrum-half Flo Robinson have full-time England contracts for the first time, having been named among 32 deals for the 2026-27 season.

Venner made her England debut in 2020 as a 17-year-old, but had to wait five years before picking up her second cap against Italy in the 2025 Six Nations.

Despite finishing as joint-top try-scorer in the 2024-25 PWR season, she missed out on selection for the World Cup.

However, Vennuer was part of the squad that won an eighth straight Six Nations this year, appearing in wins over Scotland and Italy as head coach John Mitchell experimented with his back-three options.

Robinson, also 24, provides specialist scrum-half cover for Natasha Hunt and Lucy Packer, meaning Claudia Moloney-MacDonald and Helena Rowland, who have been primed to step in at nine in the past, are unlikely to have to swap in from their more accustomed positions in the back line.

Lilli Ives Campion, who found herself as England's most experienced second row after a raft of injuries and absences during the Six Nations, is also rewarded with a first full-time contract.

Teenager Demelza Short, who made four appearances and two starts in that campaign, is one of six players awarded a transition contract.

Zoe Stratford, Abbie Ward and Rosie Galligan, who are all due to give birth later this year, and hooker Lark Atkin-Davies, who welcomed a daughter in June, are all included.

Marlie Packer, who scored seven tries during England's Six Nations campaign, is one of three veterans from the Red Roses' World Cup triumphs of both 2014 and 2025, along with Hunt and back row Alex Matthews.

"Today's announcement recognises a group of competitive and committed players who continue to drive standards every day and represent what this team is all about, as evidenced by our achievements in the 2025-26 season," said Charlie Hayter, England Rugby's head of women's performance.

"Competition within this squad remains incredibly fierce, and that's one of our greatest strengths."

England play Australia, Canada and New Zealand in Manchester, Exeter and London respectively in September, before two Tests against Canada and one against the United States on the other side of the Atlantic in October.

Their pursuit of a record-extending ninth successive Six Nations title begins away to Wales on 10 April.

title: Norrie beats Tomic at Los Cabos Open in 50 minutes
description: Cameron Norrie's resurgent form continues as he overpowers Bernard Tomic in just 50 minutes to progress to the semi-finals of the Los Cabos Open in Mexico.
fullText:
Cameron Norrie's resurgent form continued as he overpowered Bernard Tomic in just 50 minutes to progress to the semi-finals of the Los Cabos Open in Mexico.

Fifth-seed Norrie won 12 straight games to defeat his Australian opponent 6-1 6-0 and set up a semi-final meeting with defending champion Denis Shapovalov.

The British number two travelled to Mexico on a run of six consecutive defeats, having not won a match since April, but has put together a run of three successive straight-set victories.

He defeated Aleksandar Kovacevic comfortably in the first round before recovering from 3-0 down in the first set to beat James Duckworth in the second round.

"I'm pleased with the result. I was very solid, I returned well, I made a lot of tough balls when I needed to, and I kept him moving," said Norrie.

"I enjoyed the match, and it's nice to go to bed a little bit earlier."

The other semi-final will be contested by Hong Kong's Coleman Wong and Frenchman Arthur Gea, both of whom are ATP Tour semi-final debutants.

Tomic, 33, who reached the main draw as a lucky loser from qualifying, held serve in the opening game of the match against Norrie but then lost the rest.

Norrie said it had taken him a while to get his confidence back following his run of losses, adding he had also "overtrained a little bit" before his first-round exit at the French Open in May.

"To get a win here meant a lot," he said. "I took a lot of confidence from that and I was just able to play, not thinking about too much, just enjoying myself,"

In the Washington Open, top seed Jessica Pegula overcame a slow start to beat Poland's Magdalena Frech 3-6 6-3 6-0 in the second round on Thursday.

American Pegula, 32, saved five of seven break points on her own serve before sealing victory, and will face fifth seed Anna Kalinskaya of Russia in the quarter-finals of the WTA 500 event on Friday.

Second seed Elina Svitolina also booked her place in the quarter-finals with a 7-6 (7-4) 6-4 win over Uzbekistan's Polina Kudermetova.

title: 'Relieved' Woods wins gold again in restaged race
description: Scotland's Melanie Woods wins the Commonwealth Games women's 1500m T54 for the second time in under 40 hours after streaking to victory in the restaged final.
fullText:
Scotland's Melanie Woods has won the Commonwealth Games women's 1500m T54 for the second time in under 40 hours after streaking to victory in the restaged final - however England's Ellis Kottas could not replicate her silver medal.

Woods set a new Games record to triumph in Glasgow on Wednesday evening, but it emerged on Thursday morning that Para-athletics authorities had decided the race should be held again following appeals surrounding a first-lap crash.

However, the Scot kept her composure in her home city to replicate her initial success, break the record again, and reclaim the gold that was already hers - in mind if not around her neck.

Kottas, though, finished fourth, having said she was "low-key traumatised" when it became known that the race result was overturned.

"I'm happy, I'm excited, but it feels like relief, to be honest," Woods told BBC Sport Scotland, after backing up the triumph with a win in her 400m heat 90 minutes later.

"It's created a bit of a storyline and I feel like people have been following for the plot, so I'm just happy to be able to do it again.

Woods led from the start in her home city, although Noemi Alphonse of Mauritius and Australia's Eliza Ault-Connell kept her honest over the first couple of laps.

The latter had fallen away by the final 200m, though, and the Scot held off the Mauritian as she was roared by down the home straight by the crowd to finish in a time almost a second quicker than she did on Wednesday.

"It was in my mind 'what have I got left?' and you do question what you've got in your arms," she said.

"But I just needed to be confident I could stay out in front and it was nice coming down the home straight and not seeing her wheel moving in front of me."

Woods - who has used a wheelchair since being hit by a car while riding her bike in 2018 - had celebrated her success at Scotstoun swathed in a Saltire on Wednesday.

It was not until she left the track, heard the chatter and saw people scurrying into the officials' office that she realised there might be an issue and went "into self-protection mode".

Uncertainly cloaked the rest of the evening until it was decreed around midnight that she would have to go and win gold all over again.

"There was obviously a bit of disappointment and I wasn't able to celebrate fully," she added. "It definitely dampened the excitement but I just had to park that and come out and do it again today.

"I'm pretty good at compartmentalising and trying not to ride the wave of the ups and the downs. I'm no stranger to that and it's not something I've dealt with before."

Woods had conducted similar interviews on Wednesday, talking about being the gold medallist. So was she sure this time that the prize was definitely hers?

"If they call me back for a rerun, I'm not doing it..."

title: Rugby v cricket - England's George swaps sports to help tackle MND
description: England and Saracens' Jamie George on why he and Somerset's Lewis Gregory are playing a charity cricket match to raise money for motor neurone disease charities.
fullText:
Rugby might be England and Saracens hooker Jamie George's first love but cricket is still a regular part of his sporting life and career.

It's why he and his club team-mates did not need much persuading to 

"We [Saracens] do play [cricket] - our warm-up [for] every rugby session - summer, winter, snowing, rain - is one hand, one bounce," George told BBC Radio Somerset.

"The boys love it because they're mad-keen cricket fans."

George will skipper 'Team Rugby' for the game on 19 August at the County Ground in Taunton, in a side that also includes current and former England internationals Owen Farrell, Elliot Daly, Ben Earl and Max Malins.

Somerset captain Lewis Gregory will lead the opposition to tie in with his testimonial year, with Surrey and England's Jamie Overton and former Somerset all-rounder Peter Trego also on the teamsheet.

George was in the stand at the County Ground for a T20 match earlier this season and bumped into Somerset all-rounder Tom Kohler-Cadmore, who was injured at the time, and the idea was touted.

"I'm actually doing a testimonial year next year and I said the dream would be to play a game of cricket somewhere like this," George, who captained England during this summer's Nations Series, said.

"[Kohler-Cadmore] said: 'Why don't we do it for Lewis' testimonial?' I thought it's an unbelievable opportunity."

Back with his Saracens team, George instantly started pulling a side together.

"We were out to dinner and within seconds we were coming up with a batting order," he said.

"I suggested we should merge teams and they said 'no, we want to take them on', categorically rugby versus cricket."

While George and his team-mates are not short of experience, with hundreds of international caps and English Prem games between them, on the cricket pitch it is, of course, a different story compared to their opponents.

However, the rugby squad do have some experience to call upon.

Daly represented Surrey as a teenager and played for England at age-grade level, while Earl similarly played for Kent as an under-15.

"They're both very handy so at least we'll get some runs on the board and then we'll have to scramble around a bit," George, 35, said.

As for what kind of player George will be? "Like a Daren Sammy [former West Indies T20 World Cup-winning captain] type role, I would not bowl and I'd bat at nine or 10 and just be there for morale," he said.

"I'm an old man now but I used to play a lot of cricket back when I was at school."

Gregory, who is Somerset's all-time leading T20 wicket-taker, is happy the game is being played on his turf rather than the other way around and in a rugby match.

"A lot of our lads are excited to see the rugby boys in action and it will be nice to put them under a bit of pressure rather than it being in a rugby game, because that could be a little bit messy," he said.

The decision to support the MND Association was also an easy one for both Gregory and George, with former players in both rugby and cricket having been diagnosed with the disease in recent years.

MND is a neurological condition which affects the brain and spinal cord, and can affect a person's ability to talk, walk and breathe.

Former England and Gloucestershire fast bowler David 'Syd' Lawrence died in 2025, having been diagnosed with MND the year previously.

Doddie Weir, the former Scotland lock, died in 2022, six years after being diagnosed with MND, and having raised millions of pounds and awareness to combat the disease, while former Gloucester lock Ed Slater and former England captain Lewis Moody both live with MND.

"It's a horrible disease and that's why the rugby and the cricket communities are very similar, there's a lot of crossover between the two," George said.

"We look after our own and we want to try to do everything we can to raise as much awareness and hopefully find a cure."

title: Chelsea fined £10m for breaching agent rules
description: Chelsea are fined £10m by the Football Association for breaching rules relating to payments to agents between 2009 and 2022.
fullText:
Chelsea have been fined £10m and given a suspended ban from registering new players for two transfer windows for breaching rules relating to payments to agents between 2009 and 2022.

But the club have had a six-point deduction, which was suspended until 30 June 2027, "set aside" on appeal.

Owners Todd Boehly and Clearlake Capital self-reported 74 breaches of FA rules when they purchased the club in 2022.

Chelsea admitted making £47m in secret payments to unregistered agents and third-parties over transfers between 2011 and 2018.

The £10m Chelsea have been fined will be invested into grassroots football.

In March, they received an immediate nine-month academy transfer ban and a £750,000 fine over the registration of academy players between 2019 and 2022.

title: League has 'genuine concern' for members over cheating claim
description: An amateur cricket league says it has "genuine concern for the welfare" of Saltburn Cricket Club members over a recent finger clicking controversy that has made global headlines.
fullText:
An amateur cricket league has expressed its "genuine concern for the welfare" of Saltburn Cricket Club members over a recent finger clicking controversy that has made global headlines.

The North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League spoke out in the wake of worldwide interest in an alleged incident that has led to a player being suspended by the club.

That happened after a video from the second XI Division 2 game involving Saltburn and Norton went viral on social media.

The video appeared to show Saltburn fielder Brian Devine clicking his fingers in order to trick the umpire into giving a Norton batter out.

On Monday, the North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League began an investigation into Devine, who has been suspended by Saltburn for the "foreseeable future".

The league said it is treating allegations of cheating "with the utmost seriousness", and in a statement on Friday called for the "rights of all parties" to be observed in the face of intense scrutiny on social media.

"We would want to place on record our genuine concern for the welfare for those at Saltburn Cricket Club and ask for all to take that into account - there are many people at the club and one of our aims will be to provide them with any wellbeing support we can," the league said.

"Whilst we understand, to some degree, the interest this issue has generated in the press and media, it is imperative that now this process is under way that the rights of all parties are observed, including the overriding principles of natural justice and a right to a fair hearing for any individual or any entity concerned.

"Anything less risks prejudicing any formal actions which may follow."

The incident has been dubbed 'Clicky Ponting' - a pun on the name of former Australia captain Ricky Ponting.

Saltburn, in their own statement on Wednesday, said: "We believe that the club acted decisively as soon as the complaint and investigation were made known to us.

"The player at the centre of the complaint has been suspended and will not play again for the club this season or in the forseeable future, pending the outcome of this investigation."

That statement added: "This has been a very distressing and stressful experience for all those concerned, and we would ask that this reality is borne in mind and that personal boundaries are respected, as we are an amateur club entirely run by volunteers."

title: Will Scottish Premiership return to two-team title tussle?
description: A new Scottish Premiership season begins on Friday, but will anyone match Heart of Midlothian from last term and challenge Celtic and Rangers for the title?
fullText:
And in the relative blink of an eye, the new Scottish Premiership season is upon us with much to live up to compared to last time, an epic campaign that looked like making the impossible possible for month upon month.

How Scotland, and other parts of the world, became entranced by the fairytale only for the reality of sport's essential brutality to hit them square between the eyes at Celtic Park on denouement day.

If there is a non-Glasgow team capable of roughing up the big two as Heart of Midlothian did repeatedly last season then we're in for a wild ride.

If this league campaign goes to the final three minutes on the final day, if the domestic football story to beat all domestic football stories is in touching distance as the campaign swings for home next spring then we'll be blessed.

If. Nobody will be betting a brass farthing on history repeating itself, though. True, nobody really saw Hearts coming last time, but does lightning strike twice?

Listen: Scottish Premiership is back - season preview

Scottish Premiership is back - here's why you shouldn't miss it

Who has your Premiership club brought in & let go this summer?

Hearts are in transition under new management and a raft of new players in the post-Derek McInnes, Lawrence Shankland age. They'll take time to settle.

Is there a different bolter out there? Motherwell, so easy on the eye last season, have had their guts ripped out in the summer and are also rebuilding, albeit playing with the same easy style as before.

Aberdeen? It would take a brave soul to support any claim for an Old Firm-challenging run, but in Stephen Robinson's first full season, they should go a whole lot better than last term.

Hibernian have the potential to push hard for third, but consistency problems follow them around year upon year. Falkirk, the other top-six club, would see a repeat of last season as a fantastic outcome, which it would be.

The plaintive cry is that young Scottish footballers get a chance to play a part in all this, that clubs trust their youth for a change. It's an appeal made this time every year and, for the most part, ignored.

We look to be back in the realms of a two-horse race and the two horses have experienced jockeys now, not two Old Firm apprentices like Russell Martin and Wilfried Nancy.

Hearts did so many outstanding things in taking the race to the wire, but both of those hapless characters helped them on their way. In Martin O'Neill and McInnes, the capacity for Celtic and Rangers slapstick, and that of an outsider causing them tremors, has been dramatically reduced.

The surreal cameos of Martin and Nancy and Hearts' thrilling surge that reverberated around the UK, Europe and parts of the wider world were just a few of things that made last season unmatchable in terms of drama and genuine gobsmacking moments.

The fall of Brendan Rodgers, and Dermot Desmond's startling evisceration of a celebrated manager, could only be rivalled if Celtic's major shareholder suddenly takes a flamethrower to his relationship with O'Neill.

Desmond's son, Ross, thought it a good idea to declare football war on the club's own supporters at an annual meeting that was promptly cancelled. On the really dark side, Peter Lawwell, the titan of 20 years at Parkhead, left while citing intolerable abuse of a section of the support that lost the run of themselves.

O'Neill's return was astonishing, his second return almost every bit as remarkable. Danny Rohl came and went at Rangers. Jimmy Thelin exited Aberdeen. St Mirren won a League Cup in thrilling circumstances and then almost got themselves relegated. Everybody fell in love with Jens Berthel Askou's Motherwell. Praise was heaped on the quality of Falkirk's football.

At the start of the season nobody foresaw much, if any, of this. What was more predictable then, as it is now, is the toxic nature of some of what goes around the biggest games.

As a club, Hearts have every right to remain livid at the crass goading of their players during the invasion that greeted Celtic's title win - and the tokenistic sanction that followed it.

The Scottish FA's independent review of the disgraceful scenes before, during and after the Old Firm Cup tie at Ibrox in March was thunderously critical of all parties - clubs, governing bodies, police.

Their recommendation, one of many, was that the SFA and Scottish Professional Football League start to get serious with stand closures and then stadium closures as a direct consequence of misbehaviour. Enough is enough was the mantra.

How long before the mettle of the governing bodies is tested? And how long before the independent report, in the face of resistance from the most powerful clubs in the land, is quietly forgotten about?

In the coming seasons, the narratives don't just begin and end on the pitch. The off-pitch stuff is compelling, too.

The standards of refereeing will be under the microscope like never before after the contentious and title-defining calls came in a mad flurry at the end of last season. We want the drama and the storylines of much of the campaign just gone, but we could do without the poisonous way it all finished in the final week or two.

Controversial decisions, threats to officials, a noxious atmosphere culminating with Celtic fans squaring up to Hearts players - it was a pitiful end to what been a thrilling season.

There will be surprises ahead, but at this remove it's hard to argue against the familiar sight of old rivals going head-to-head for the title.

The Celtic board spent much of last season and practically every day of the summer getting monstered by elements among their own support. They have, though, delivered two significant signings for huge money - Kasper Hogh and Camilo Duran.

Hogh is the pedigree striker that Celtic have lacked since Kyogo Furuhashi was around. Duran is more of a replacement for Daizen Maeda. At a reported £17m for the pair, Celtic have flexed their fiscal muscle.

There is consistent talk that midfielder Arne Engels and right-back Alistair Johnston might be leaving, so the Celtic of this week might still look considerably different to the Celtic of the coming months.

Even with another few comings and goings they're still the most settled side in the country - and the most proven. Fit-again centre-half Cameron Carter-Vickers will be like a new signing. If winger Jota can make a return to something close to his old self then Celtic will be hard to contain.

Rangers, under McInnes, have added beef and leadership, doughty characters rather than the flighty articles they have been attracted to for so long. McInnes will make them organised and robust.

Whether they have the creative wit to go with the physicality is another question. In Scottish terms, Rangers' American owners have spent colossal money, splurging tens of millions on the creation of a team, and an environment, that can win a league and do something in Europe.

From Martin's capricious management to the cold-blooded pragmatism of McInnes is some leap for Rangers. McInnes has broad shoulders, which is just as well, because there's a heavy burden of expectation there. There's enormous pressure on him.

He'll see it as an opportunity, of course. The biggest of his managerial life.

O'Neill versus McInnes looks to be the story of the season, unless there's another delicious sub-plot lurking in the long grass.

title: AI labels to be compulsory on authentic-looking content under EU rules
description:
Companies must ensure people know when they are interacting with artificially generated images, audio and text designed to look real
From apparently conspiring to steal elections to abusing staff or performing embarrassing dance moves, the last few years have seen plenty of fake content made about politicians intended to malign its targets and mislead the public.
Now EU rules aim to stem the flood of this deceptive content: starting from Sunday, artificially generated images, audio and text designed to look authentic must be labelled.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Companies must ensure people know when they are interacting with artificially generated images, audio and text designed to look real

From apparently conspiring to steal elections to abusing staff or performing embarrassing dance moves, the last few years have seen plenty of fake content made about politicians intended to malign its targets and mislead the public.

Now EU rules aim to stem the flood of this deceptive content: starting from Sunday, artificially generated images, audio and text designed to look authentic must be labelled.

The rules, devised under the EU’s landmark AI Act, mean companies must ensure people know when they are interacting with an AI-powered chatbot or viewing a manipulated image or AI-generated text.

The rules apply to new AI systems on the EU market from 2 August, while existing ones have an extra four months to comply.

“It is a matter not only of customer protection, it’s also a matter of democracy protection,” the Green MEP Sergey Lagodinsky, who helped negotiate the AI Act, told the Guardian. “Making transparent this information is something which we need to preserve our democracy and the authenticity of facts online.”

Under the rules, synthetic text, images, video and audio designed to look truthful must be visibly marked as AI-generated and contain a digital watermark to show the artificial origins of the content.

Texts on matters of public interest must also be labelled as AI-made if there is no human editorial oversight.

Companies are encouraged to label AI-generated content pre-dating the rules, although this is not compulsory. The rules will not apply to users’ personal content and there is an exemption for “evidently artistic”, satirical and fictional works.

Failure to comply could result in fines of up to €15m (£12.8) or 3% of a company’s worldwide global turnover.

The EU executive has created black-and-white labels anyone can use, although companies can design their own.

Deepfakes have included audio purporting to reveal the Slovakian opposition leader Michal Šimečka conspiring with a journalist to rig elections, mocked-up videos of the French president, Emmanuel Macron, dancing in a 1980s nightclub, and fake footage of the then UK Labour leader, Keir Starmer, abusing party staff.

The tech industry says it supports the quest to make deepfakes visible, but fears the rules will be interpreted too broadly and overwhelm internet users with banners and labels.

The Computer and Communications Industry Association argues that EU guidelines published in July have expanded the definition of a deepfake far beyond the 2024 AI Act.

“The label was meant to flag deceptive content,” said CCIA Europe’s AI policy lead, Boniface de Champris. “That distinction has been removed, so now almost everything gets labelled – a landscape in an advert is the same as a manipulated political speech. Like cookie banners, once labels are everywhere, users stop noticing them. That doesn’t protect anyone, it just burdens commercial activity across the board.”

He thinks the most visible change for the public will not be on social media, which “already labels most AI content” but “in areas where AI is already used at scale but people don’t know it – advertising, film, publishing”.

“Expect a lot more labels in sectors not usually associated with AI, and the burden will fall hardest on those least versed in AI regulation,” De Champris said.

Some of the world’s largest tech companies already have policies designed to inform users about AI-generated content.

TikTok, for example, says it requires creators to label realistic AI-generated images, audio and video, and that it has helped label more than 3bn pieces of content. However, recent research has shown that AI-generated doctors are gaining millions of views on TikTok by spreading dubious health advice.

Google launched a tool called SynthID in 2023, which enables users to check if an image is AI-generated. The company says it has put an invisible digital watermark, which enables identification, on more than 100bn images and 60,000 years’ worth of audio.

Google and Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, have signed a voluntary code of practice intended to help companies comply with the EU’s AI transparency rules.

The European Commission said more than 180 organisations had signed the code, which was drawn up by independent experts under the supervision of the EU AI office.

Signing the code is seen by regulators as a sign of good intent, while non-signatories must show they are meeting the rules in other ways.

Meta launched policies in 2024 to help people identify AI-generated photo-realistic images. It says it has been developing industry-wide technical standards to identify AI audio and video.

Announcing Meta’s intention to sign the EU code of practice earlier this week [28 July], its vice-president for public policy in Europe, Markus Reinisch, said: “We must avoid a situation where online content is subject to a growing array of different labels and disclosures that end up overwhelming people, while at the same time adding additional regulatory complexity for providers.”

Lagodinsky, the EU lawmaker, said he believed the industry could find a way: “I have a deep respect for industry, but in all too many cases, they complain, and … then after things are implemented, it doesn’t look that burdensome to them. And there is always a solution.”

The transparency rules are part of broader enforcement of the AI Act, starting from 2 August. The commission’s lead official on tech policy, Henna Virkkunen, said AI was a “transformative technology” that could bring “extraordinary benefits” but the most advanced models “create risks on an entirely new scale”.

“Europe anticipated this development. With the AI Act, we established a clear, risk-based and durable framework for trustworthy AI —one that gives innovators legal certainty while protecting the public interest.”

title: ‘A universal human story’: Clean Start’s thought-provoking tidying sim tells immigrant’s tale
description:
Playing as recent arrival Lena, your challenges include learning a new language and uncovering family secrets – its developer hopes it will spread ‘a little more compassion’
The cosy house-sorting sim has become a much-loved staple of the PC indie scene. Titles such as Unpacking, A Little to the Left and Momento charm players with their detailed interiors and quiet narratives of lives lived and shared within the same four walls. For Clean Start, Polish developer Serious Sim has taken a different approach – here you play as domestic cleaner, Lena, an immigrant who has arrived in an unspecified western country with little knowledge of the local language, and a family to support back home.
From here, you’re tasked with cleaning a series of houses and apartments, polishing tables, tidying shelves and scrubbing muddy pawprints from kitchen floors. It seems you’re able to rearrange the rooms, giving them a personal feel, which is after all one of the most pleasing elements of the genre.
fullText:
Playing as recent arrival Lena, your challenges include learning a new language and uncovering family secrets – its developer hopes it will spread ‘a little more compassion’

The cosy house-sorting sim has become a much-loved staple of the PC indie scene. Titles such as Unpacking, A Little to the Left and Momento charm players with their detailed interiors and quiet narratives of lives lived and shared within the same four walls. For Clean Start, Polish developer Serious Sim has taken a different approach – here you play as domestic cleaner, Lena, an immigrant who has arrived in an unspecified western country with little knowledge of the local language, and a family to support back home.

From here, you’re tasked with cleaning a series of houses and apartments, polishing tables, tidying shelves and scrubbing muddy pawprints from kitchen floors. It seems you’re able to rearrange the rooms, giving them a personal feel, which is after all one of the most pleasing elements of the genre. You can also, we are reassured, pet the dog.

For artist and game director Katarzyna Haptaś the game has personal meaning. “It is largely inspired by the stories my mother told about working abroad as a domestic cleaner,” she says. “But that experience was shared by many members of my family, as well as my friends’ families. Back in the 90s, there was always some kid who had a parent working elsewhere, sending packages home for Christmas. I was blessed to hear stories from my grandmother as well. She went to America with only a few dollars in her purse and no confirmation that anyone would be waiting for her at the airport. All of that at a time when there was no internet or cellphones.”

Haptaś has drawn on her own experiences, too. Working as a cleaner in a local cinema taught her how people interact with cleaning staff. The team researched the experiences of those coming to her home country to seek work. “During the pre-production phase of the prototype, we managed to have an interview with an immigration centre worker in Poland,” she says. “She shared many insights on immigrants working in Poland at the time, mainly from war-torn Ukraine.”

Interestingly, the game uses language as a key part of its challenge. While chatting to Lena, her employers use unfamiliar words that she can learn through interacting with the environment. Owners will also ask you to find specific objects, usually with sentimental value or family stories and dramas attached. “By interacting with certain objects, players can piece together clues about what’s happening in each client’s life,” says Haptaś. “Often, these items help the clients realise something important or uncover a secret that was kept from them. Depending on what the player finds, there are different lines of dialogue commenting on it. Finding the right combination of items will reveal the full story to the player.”

Clean Start isn’t just a cosy house-tidying sim – instead, it is using this genre to explore themes of connection, comfort and closure. Immigration has become such a polarising debate, there is value in such a quiet depiction. “I hope this is a universal human story,” says Haptaś. “I hope that people will see each other as human beings, with all of our shared hopes and fears. Leaving home to work in a foreign country with limited knowledge of the language is never an easy decision. It wasn’t easy in the 90s and it isn’t easy today. Ultimately, I hope that players will leave with a little more compassion and patience for those who are simply doing their best to work and communicate.”

title: My family is coming apart – so it’s time for one last video game session | Dominik Diamond
description:
I wanted our last family games night to be the best fun we’ve ever had. Maybe we should have stuck with Mario Kart …
It is the end of an era for the Diamond family. For 20 years, there have been five of us living together. It has not been easy. Militant vegan daughters, sons who have inherited Scottish tempers, and a youngest child who attracts trouble like an industrial magnet, have meant our house has been conflict-laden at times.
fullText:
I wanted our last family games night to be the best fun we’ve ever had. Maybe we should have stuck with Mario Kart …

It is the end of an era for the Diamond family. For 20 years, there have been five of us living together. It has not been easy. Militant vegan daughters, sons who have inherited Scottish tempers, and a youngest child who attracts trouble like an industrial magnet, have meant our house has been conflict-laden at times. Throw in the fact that we are beset with all manner of mental health bobbins and chronic illnesses that resulted in two of our three kids almost dying in hospitals and you get a family that is combustible – but extremely close.

Through it all, we had games. They always brought us back together. Not just us all hunkering over Super Mario Kart like some kind of UN-mandated family therapy, but the conversations that happen when any of us spy another playing something new. Games are a cultural touchstone that helped us crack through the veneer of disagreements and distrust and remind us that we have more things in common than we sometimes feel.

But now we are moving out of the house we have shared for years. My wife has to go back to the UK for family reasons, #1 Child is moving in with her boyfriend and youngest child is moving in with a friend. This leaves the Son and I – we are moving into an apartment for the next few months, which Charlie is already dubbing the bro-tel. (I am filled with equal parts excitement and dread about this.)

So I wanted one last family games night to remind us of simpler times before we all go our separate ways. I wanted it to be the best fun we have ever had. I wanted … Quiplash!

Quiplash is one of the most important games in the history of our family, because I view it as the game that trained my kids to be funny. Seeing them all become fairly high-level comedy beings has been the greatest thrill of my life as a dad.

It’s a simple “fill in the blanks or answer the question with something funny to get the most votes” game, the beauty of it being you can play using mobile phones as controllers and five people can play. That’s why I have it as a go-to. Getting any family together to do anything is like herding particularly wilful sheep, and when was the last time you saw a shepherd try that while hunting for 10 working batteries for gaming controllers? Exactly.

It’s not just the genuinely funny answers that get votes: there is also a lot of love for old family running gags, most of which are at my expense, usually my baldness or my rigidity with rules.

However, while I am impressed by my grownup kids’ quick-thinking quippery, I am still appalled by some of their spelling. So for our final game, I introduce a rule that you can only vote for answers spelt correctly. This rule is not just ignored but aggressively mocked with answers that are part punchline and part Welsh street name.

I am in last place because they can tell which answers are from me. So, I start deliberately entering badly spelt answers to confuse them, so they give up trying to play the game seriously and while I am writing quality punchlines such as “God said ‘wrong door’” (you had to be there), I am faced with answers from them such as “pee pee poo poo”.

And then the rows break out. My two youngest kids work at the same trendy bar/restaurant, and they have issues with each other. One suggested a role for the other there that they are not happy about, so they declare they never want to work in the same place together again. Impressively, during the argument, my son still manages to answer “skittle flavour that just missed the cut” with “narly Netenyahu nectarine”. Which almost got my vote until I noticed that neither Netanyahu nor gnarly are spelt like that.

The row escalates. Wife and #1 Child have reverted to doomscrolling on their phones instead. No one wants to play. It’s all falling apart. Not just this desperate attempt at one final family gaming session, but the family itself. In one week, our matriarch, the most important one of us, will be on the other side of the Atlantic. In a couple of months, #1 Child could be the only one still actually living on this side of it.

Memories start flooding back: the summer I spent playing Super Mario Sunshine with #1 Child when she was five. Evading guard dogs in the snow with my son on Call of Duty: Modern Warfare when he wasn’t much older. Seeing my youngest child fall in love with Kirby. The years of Mario Kart, Mortal Kombat and Just Dance. The conversations. The debates. The windups. There is such joy in those moments but now they are spilling through my fingers like water.

I think of all the times in recent years when one of the kids has asked me if I want to play a game with them. And I’ve been “too busy”. I wish I had all those moments back to create more memories.

My wife, ever the peacemaker of the family, declares the next day that we will have one more go at this the night before she goes back to Blighty. That prospect seems as good as it gets right now.

title: Tasklet (YC P26) Is Hiring a Customer Success Engineer
description: Our users are building real automations with Tasklet — connecting dozens of services, writing complex workflows, and trusting an AI agent with critical work. When something breaks or gets confusing, the quality of help they get determines whether they go deeper or give up. But we don't want to solve this just by throwing people at support tickets. We want to solve it by making everything work better — through better product, better self-serve resources, smarter automation, and better internal tooling.
fullText:
Tasklet is building the AI platform companies use to run their business on agents. A customer describes an outcome in plain English, and Tasklet gets the work done across their tools and systems—immediately or in the cloud 24×7.

Our users are building real automations with Tasklet — connecting dozens of services, writing complex workflows, and trusting an AI agent with critical work. When something breaks or gets confusing, the quality of help they get determines whether they go deeper or give up. But we don't want to solve this just by throwing people at support tickets. We want to solve it by making everything work better — through better product, better self-serve resources, smarter automation, and better internal tooling.

We’re looking for someone to become a core owner of our customer-facing work: handle inbound support, talk live with users, proactively help high-value customers get more out of Tasklet, and relentlessly automate and improve the system so your workload keeps going down while our customers keep getting more successful.

This is a great role for someone with roughly 1–5 years of experience who is a technology power user, great with customers, and excited to grow into a broad customer-facing role at an AI startup.

Competitive benefits (medical, dental, vision, 401k, 4 weeks PTO, free lunch, etc.)

title: States ranked by how much of their federal income tax is paid by the top 1%
description: See how much the top 1% of earners pay in federal income taxes in every US state, ranked using the latest available IRS data.
fullText:
Tax proposals in New York and California aim to increase taxes on the wealthiest residents.

A SmartAsset study calculated how much of each state's federal income taxes was paid by the top 1%.

The top 1% of earners make 19% of incomes in the US but pay 37% of all federal income taxes.

Tax proposals targeting wealthy residents have renewed debate in states including New York and California about how much the rich should be paying in taxes. But just how much do the top 1% already pay?

While state and local taxes vary widely across states, from high-tax states like California to no-state-income-tax states like Florida and Nevada, federal income tax rates are the same across all US states.

A recent SmartAsset study examined the total federal individual income tax paid by residents of each state and calculated the share paid by the state's top 1% of households.

Individual income taxes are the largest source of revenue for the federal government. That tax revenue helps fund government programs and services, as well as interest on the national debt.

For tax year 2026, federal marginal income-tax rates range from 10% on taxable income of up to $12,400 for single filers and $24,800 for married couples filing jointly, to 37% on taxable income above $640,600 for single filers and $768,700 for married couples filing jointly.

Across the country, the top 1% of earners made an average of 19.5% of all income but paid 37% of federal individual income taxes, SmartAsset found.

SmartAsset ranked all 50 states by the percentage of federal income tax collected that is paid by the top 1% of earners, using the most recent personal income tax return data from the IRS covering the tax year 2022. SmartAsset treated each return as one household.

title: ICE lodges detainer for illegal immigrant accused of trying to disarm Virginia police officer
description: ICE lodged a detainer against a Honduran national who allegedly ambushed and tried to disarm a Fairfax County police officer in Annandale, Virginia.
fullText:
Federal immigration officials have lodged a detainer against a Honduran national accused of attempting to disarm a police officer during an encounter in Northern Virginia.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is asking Fairfax County officials not to release Nehemia Noel Fuentes-Banegas after authorities said he ambushed a Fairfax County police officer Tuesday.

According to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), officers responded to a report of a man who left a home in Annandale following an argument while allegedly armed with two knives.

Spanberger's Ice Rollback To Blame For Toddler Killing, Virginia 'Hotbed' Of Illegal Immigrant Crime: Dhs

Fairfax County police said the man also stabbed himself before leaving the residence and fleeing into a nearby wooded area.

As officers searched a wooded area, Fuentes-Banegas allegedly emerged from the brush, grabbed an officer's firearm and attempted to disarm the officer, DHS said.

Fairfax County police said one officer fired his service weapon while a second officer simultaneously deployed a department-issued Taser. The bullet grazed Fuentes-Banegas' shoulder, police said.

Fuentes-Banegas was arrested and charged with attempted disarming of a law enforcement officer. ICE has lodged a detainer requesting that Fairfax County notify federal authorities before his release.

Illegal Alien 'Monster' Charged With Raping Dead Girlfriend's Daughter, Dhs Blames Biden-era Policies

According to DHS, Fuentes-Banegas entered the United States illegally through Texas in 2022 and was later released under the Biden administration.

"This criminal illegal alien from Honduras attacked a law enforcement officer and attempted to take the officer's gun," DHS Assistant Secretary Tricia McLaughlin said in a statement.

"He has now been charged with attempted disarming of a law enforcement officer," she continued. "ICE is calling on Governor Abigail Spanberger and her fellow sanctuary politicians to commit to not releasing this dangerous criminal from jail."

DHS blamed Virginia's sanctuary policies for limiting cooperation with federal immigration authorities, arguing they have made the commonwealth "a magnet for illegal alien crime."

Abigail Spanberger's Virginia A 'Hotbed' For Illegal Immigrant Crime, Dhs Says After Latest Rape Charge

The department noted that Spanberger signed executive orders at the start of her administration ending former Gov. Glenn Youngkin's 287(g) agreements and limiting state cooperation with ICE.

"Under Governor Spanberger, Virginia has become a hotbed of illegal alien crime," DHS said.

DHS also pointed to the recent arrest of Raul Genesis Ortiz Moran, a Mexican national charged with second-degree murder and aggravated sexual battery in connection with the death of a 2-year-old girl in Louisa County.

"This horrific tragedy was completely avoidable because this illegal alien should have never been in our country. Governor Spanberger's sanctuary policies have made Virginia a hotbed for illegal alien crime," DHS Assistant Secretary Lauren Bis previously told Fox News Digital.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Spanberger's office for comment.

Fox News Digital's Charles Creitz contributed to this report.

title: First flesh-eating bacteria death of 2026 recorded in this state
description: Infections caused by vibrio vulnificus are contracted through eating raw seafood or swimming in contaminated water.
fullText:
Florida has reported the first death of the year caused by an infection from so-called "flesh-eating" bacterium, according to state health officials.

Vibrio vulnificus, most commonly spread through raw seafood or contact with brackish coastal water, earned its "flesh-eating" moniker from its ability to cause an infection called vibriosis that damages or "eats away" at skin and tissue. Florida records infections each year, usually resulting in a handful of deaths. Severe weather events that cause flooding, such as hurricanes Helene and Ian, have been associated with higher rates of illness and death from the bacterium.

The state has recorded 12 cases so far this season as of July 30, according to Florida Health data, and one death in Palm Beach County. It reported a total of 33 cases and five deaths in 2025.

While vibrio vulnificus infections are rare, they can quickly develop into a more serious illness, especially in people who have weakened immune systems. Serious illness and death can occur in a matter of days, and 1 in 5 people who contract the infection will die, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

An average of 100 to 200 cases of vibriosis caused by vibrio vulnificus are reported in the United States each year, with most of them in Gulf Coast states, according to CDC data. Infections caused by other types of vibrio bacteria are more common, tallying about 80,000 cases annually.

The risk to the public remains low, but experts have advised that people in coastal areas exercise extra caution while enjoying the waning days of summer. Here's what to know.

Vibrio vulnificus is a bacterium that causes a serious infection called vibriosis. Different types of vibrio bacteria cause different infections, with vibrio vulnificus causing the "most serious forms of vibriosis," according to the Cleveland Clinic.

The potentially fatal infection can quickly result in tissue damage and spreading blisters, low blood pressure, fever, organ damage, sepsis and death.

Vibrio vulnificus is often referred to as "flesh-eating" because it can also cause necrotizing fasciitis, a bacterial infection that destroys muscle and skin tissue, causing flesh around wounds to die, according to the CDC. Vibrio vulnificus is not considered the most common cause of necrotizing fasciitis in the United States, however.

The bacteria and resulting infections are rare but can be life-threatening. Without treatment, patients can die in just a few days.

Vibrio vulnificus requires salt water for survival and thrives in warm, brackish water where a stream or river meets seawater, according to the CDC.

Most infections occur when contaminated water is swallowed or gets into an open wound, such as a cut or scrape. It can enter through broken skin but cannot penetrate unharmed skin.

Vibrio vulnificus can also enter your body when you eat uncooked or undercooked shellfish, especially oysters. Raw oysters and other seafood, along with seawater exposure, are the most common sources of vibrio outbreaks tracked by the CDC.

Once inside the body, the infection can spread to the blood and organs, usually within a matter of hours.

Symptoms of a vibrio vulnificus infection begin suddenly and quickly, usually less than 24 hours after exposure, according to the CDC and the Cleveland Clinic.

A red, warm or swollen patch of skin or rash that spreads quickly and causes pain

Fluid-filled blisters and skin discoloration

Low blood pressure (often indicated by weakness, dizziness, fatigue and fainting)

Confusion or altered mental state

When consuming seafood, the CDC advises, you should:

Cook seafood, including oysters, before consuming.

Thoroughly clean surfaces that may have come in contact with raw seafood and its drippings.

Thoroughly wash your hands after handling raw seafood. If you are at high risk, wear gloves.

Avoid entering salt water or brackish water if you have any open wounds. That includes recent surgical sites, fresh tattoos and piercings, and even minor cuts or scrapes.

Cover any open wounds if you may come into contact with coastal waters or raw seafood, even if you don't plan to be directly exposed to either. Exposure can also occur during flooding caused by storms.

Immediately wash any area of open skin with soap and running water after contact with coastal water or raw seafood.

If you are at increased risk (people with weakened immune systems and conditions like liver disease, diabetes and kidney failure), wear protective shoes and clothes when in or near coastal waters.

Contributing: Janet Loehrke, USA TODAY; C. A. Bridges, USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida
