title: GOP Senate nominee ends press conference after questions on ties to White nationalist influencer
description: Republican Senate candidate Mike Collins ended a press conference Thursday after repeatedly declining to answer questions about his relationship with a son-in-law who promoted White nationalist ideolo...
fullText:
Republican Senate candidate Mike Collins ended a press conference Thursday after repeatedly declining to answer questions about his relationship with a son-in-law who promoted White nationalist ideology and circulated antisemitic content online, as first revealed by CNN's KFile.

Collins, a two-term congressman from Georgia, was appearing at Monroe County Hospital to outline his health care priorities.

But reporters pressed him to address online statements from his son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, and whether Scheer had done business or campaign work for him. Collins said the matter had been "fully addressed" and pivoted to attacking Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff.

"You know, we've fully addressed that," Collins said. "But Jon Ossoff refuses to disavow these democrat socialist movements in our country."

Collins then criticized Ossoff over transgender rights, federal spending, immigration, bail policies and what he called "radical anti-Israel extremists."

The questions followed a CNN KFile investigation into Scheer, who is married to Collins' daughter, Summer.

CNN found that Scheer had used his large social media following to promote White nationalist ideology, share antisemitic conspiracy theories and circulate Nazi imagery. He has also called for Muslims to be deported and shared material promoting Patriot Front, a White supremacist group.

Scheer has appeared in family photographs on Collins' campaign website and social media and attended Collins' Senate primary election-night party. Voter and property records reviewed by CNN indicate that Scheer is registered to vote at a Collins-owned house adjacent to the congressman's estate in Jackson, Georgia.

One of those photos was removed following CNN's reporting. Collins told the Atlanta Journal-Constitution it was a "personal decision" to remove the photo.

At a press conference on Thursday in Washington, DC, Ossoff blasted Collins for not answering questions.

"The congressman still, two weeks later, refuses to answer whether he or his businesses paid this neo-Nazi," Ossoff said. "And today, facing these questions from the press corps in Georgia, Congressman Mike Collins ran away. He is refusing to answer questions, and Georgians have a right to know the answers."

Scheer also appears to have narrated promotional videos for Collins' trucking company. In one social media post filmed in front of trucks, Scheer said he was producing videos for a "client." CNN asked Collins' campaign whether Scheer had worked for the company as an employee, contractor or in another capacity, and whether he had a role in Collins' campaign.

Collins declined to answer repeated questions from reporters on Thursday, including if Scheer has done any paid work for his businesses or his campaign.

"Could you address the question regarding antisemitism?" one person interjected.

Collins continued criticizing Ossoff. As a reporter asked what role Scheer had played in Collins' campaign, Collins said voters would "choose to get rid of" Ossoff in November.

"Could you address his question, please, sir?" another reporter asked.

When Collins ended the press conference, a person asked, "You don't want to talk about your son-in-law at all? You want to embrace him in the family? Share his views?"

title: Trump says agreement has been reached for ‘complete disarmament’ of Hamas; Hamas has yet to respond
description: President Donald Trump on Thursday announced what he described as a historic agreement to secure the disarmament of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza.
fullText:
President Donald Trump on Thursday announced what he described as a historic agreement to secure the disarmament of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza.

As of early Thursday evening, Hamas had not confirmed the deal. CNN has reached out for comment.

"Today, the Board of Peace reached a HISTORIC agreement for the COMPLETE DISARMAMENT of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. "This is a monumental step toward lasting PEACE and SECURITY."

Disarming Hamas is a critical step in implementing Trump's multi-phase peace plan to end the war in Gaza and moving to set up a technocratic government for the strip. Mediators have been trying to negotiate with Hamas for months on implanting the plan, but there is skepticism in the region that Hamas will hold up its end of the bargain.

Earlier this month, Hamas announced that it would dissolve its government in Gaza, a move that experts say put pressure on Israel as progress from the US-brokered ceasefire plan stalled. Their statement on the move made no mention of disarmament.

CNN has reached out to the Israeli prime minister's office for comment.

Trump said the agreement would pave the way for Gaza to be governed by "a new Palestinian government" working alongside his Board of Peace, while ensuring "Israel will have the security it deserves, with Gaza no longer used as a base for terror attacks."

Trump asserted that the agreement would be implemented in phases. As armed groups are disarmed, he wrote, Israeli forces will withdraw and an International Stabilization Force, working alongside a new Palestinian police force, will assume responsibility for security in Gaza.

The president thanked mediators from Egypt, Qatar and Turkey, as well as his administration, for helping broker the agreement.

"The threat that emerged from Gaza on October 7 will NOT be allowed to rebuild!" Trump wrote, adding, "Under this agreement, Gaza will finally be in the hands of a new Palestinian government that serves its PEOPLE."

"CONGRATULATIONS TO ALL ON THIS AMAZING DEVELOPMENT, THAT EVERYBODY SAID COULD NEVER BE ACHIEVED!" Trump concluded.

CNN's Kevin Liptak and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.

title: 10 Hacks Every Samsung Galaxy User Should Know
description: There's a lot to explore on Samsung Galaxy handsets, from notification light effects to a hidden wifi menu.
fullText:
If you own an Android phone, it's more likely to be a Samsung Galaxy handset than anything else—Samsung is comfortably ahead of the likes of Google, Xiaomi, and others when it comes to global market share. And if you've got a Galaxy, you've got access to a selection of features you won't find on other Android devices.

Samsung has added a bunch of its own ideas and settings on top of Google's mobile operating system, and if you want to make the most of your Galaxy, you need to know about them. Here are some of the best ways to hack your Samsung Galaxy experience.

Why keep changing the settings on your phone if your phone can do it for you? Routines is a Galaxy utility that will wait for certain triggers and then take certain actions—one example would be turning on Do Not Disturb mode whenever you reach the office, then turning it off again when you leave.

Head to Settings then pick Modes and Routines. The first screen is Modes—specific notification settings for sleeping, working out, gaming, and so on—but if you switch to the Routines tab you can start adding some new automations.

The available triggers include times, places, specific wifi networks (like home or the office), connected devices (such as headphones), and events (like incoming notifications). Actions to take cover everything from specific Do Not Disturb modes and display settings to tasks inside apps (such as creating calendar events) and accessibility options.

If you haven't explored the Edge Panel feature much, you might not have realized just how capable it is. It's not just for shortcuts to apps—you can also add shortcuts to your favorite contacts, which is potentially even more useful.

From Settings, select Display > Edge Panels, then activate the feature via the toggle switch and tap Panels. Make sure the People panel is selected, and use the Edit button to select specific contacts. Tap the three dots then Reorder to put the contacts panel first.

There are plenty more Edge Panel customization options on these screens as well. You can choose which side of the screen it shows up on and how transparent it is, for example.

Samsung Galaxy phones can take one of your photos, apply it as the wallpaper on your device, and then dynamically adjust it based on the time of day and weather conditions—dimming the backdrop and covering it with raindrops if there's a storm at night, for instance.

You can configure this from Settings by tapping Wallpaper and style, then Change wallpapers > Create with AI > Weather. You'll need to pick an image and allow location access, and the new wallpaper will be applied to the lock screen. To make further changes to the lock screen, press and hold on it while your handset is locked. You're able to then adjust elements like the shortcuts and widgets on the display, as well as the wallpaper.

Galaxy phones come with a special brightness and vibrancy boost for watching video content, whether it's something you've saved locally or something you're streaming. From Settings, tap Advanced features > Video brightness, select Bright, and then use the toggle switches to select the apps it applies to.

Besides beeps and vibrations, notifications on Galaxy handsets can have some cool lighting effects associated with them as well. It's a fun way to make sure you see your incoming alerts, and it also can give you a quick idea of what the notifications are for.

Open Settings, then select Notifications > Notification pop-up style > Add lighting effect. You've got a choice of styles and colors to choose from, and you can set the duration for the lighting effect. For the lighting effects where you can choose a color, you can change that color based on matching keywords by selecting Lighting effect color by keyword. You could put in a contact's name and assign them a special color, for example.

This one is simple but useful: You can change what a double tap on the side button does by opening Settings and choosing Advanced features > Side button. You can have it launch the camera, the flashlight, or a specific app, for example. On the same screen, you can also adjust what a long press on the side button does—you can have it either launch one of the digital assistants installed on the phone (like Bixby or Gemini) or bring up the power menu.

There are likely to be multiple situations where you're trying to use your Samsung phone with one hand rather than two (walking the dog, carrying groceries), and that's where one-handed mode comes in.

It's enabled from Settings via Advanced features > One-handed mode, and you can then activate it by swiping down at the bottom of the screen to get a smaller, more reachable interface. Repeat the gesture again to go back to normal.

Multi Windows is another useful feature available on Samsung Galaxy phones—though it's likely to be most useful on the biggest phone displays. It lets you get two apps on screen at the same time, so you can read messages while watching a video, or whatever you want.

Swipe up from the bottom of the screen to the center to bring up the carousel of recently used apps, then swipe to your first app. Tap the app icon at the top, then Open in split screen view. You'll then be asked to choose another app to pair with it.

One of the lesser-known options on Samsung Galaxy phones is the ability to change the pixel resolution of the screen—a higher resolution means sharper text and graphics, though it will also drain your phone battery faster too, so bear that in mind.

You can configure this by selecting Display > Screen resolution from Settings. The options you'll see will depend on the specific model of handset you're using, but above the options you can see a preview of the difference each one will make.

It's a little odd that Samsung has hidden this menu away, but it's a suite of wifi diagnostics tools that you can use to check signal strength around your home, troubleshoot network problems, and check data usage. To enable the menu, which is called Connectivity Labs, open Settings and pick Connections > Wi-Fi. Tap the three dots (top right), then choose Intelligent Wi-Fi, and tap Intelligent Wi-Fi at the bottom of the screen seven times to add the extra menu.

Open Connectivity Labs and you'll see there are a host of options and features to work through. One of the most useful is the Home Wi-Fi inspection feature: Select this and your phone will guide you in measuring wifi signal strength around your home.

title: Opening night cycling joy for Wales in Velodrome
description: Wales' track cycling opening night has a bit of everything at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome.
fullText:
Wales' track cycling opening night had a bit of everything at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome.

Delight, comebacks and a little bit of despair to conclude.

Wales made the ultimate start to the track cycling campaign with a clean sweep of medals on the opening night of action at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome.

It was a day involving golden girls delivering sprint success, a medal for a returning cyclist, while her husband not given the chance to join her on the podium because one of his team-mates failed to make the start line.

Emma Finucane, Lowri Thomas and Rhian Edmunds won gold in the women's team sprint after Para-cyclist James Ball and his guide Matt Rotherham claimed silver.

Ciara Oliva helped the women's team pursuit team win bronze after coming out of retirement.

But her husband Lewis, who had also got back on the bike competitively, did not have the same opportunity after sprint team-mate Ioan Hepburn was forced to make a late withdrawal because of illness for a bronze medal race, despite making the start line.

Former Olympic silver sprint medallist Becky North and her Wales rugby legend husband George were among the Welsh crowd in attendance at the velodrome named after one of their friends.

James was a world-class sprinter in her day and Olympic champion Finucane is certainly following in her footsteps.

The trio set out their stall in the morning qualifying session by recording the fastest time and setting a new Commonwealth Games record.

It set up a battle of Britain against England trio of Katy Marchant, Sophia Capewell and Rhianna Parris-Smith and the final did not disappoint.

After Thomas led out, Finucane was installed on the second leg and responded with a trademark power turn before Edmunds held on for victory.

"Today's been insane," said Finucane.

"To qualify first was pretty nerve-wracking. We went out there and showed what we could do, but to back it up in that final, knowing we were against the strong English side was great.

"We rode our hearts out. Riding in the Welsh colours gives you that extra boost and there were so many flags in the crowd.

"When we crossed that line first, it was unbelievable."

Finucane has three events later this week scheduled. She appears to be in fine form.

Watching the girls beaming on the podium during the anthem and the support staff and other riders, shown on the big screen, belting out the words was a special sight for the golden trio.

"We stood on that top step with your team-mates singing the anthem, it's something we've all dreamed of," said Finucane.

"It is the first time I sang the anthem on that top step and the two girls were by my side belting it out.

"We also saw all my team-mates in front of us singing it with us.

"Rhian says it takes a village to do what we do. We have so many people behind the scenes you don't see on the track.

"We certainly felt that today, standing on that top step."

Just as he did in Birmingham four years ago, Ball had got, well, the ball rolling,

He competes in tandem races as an athlete with a visual impairment and is a multiple world champion across the tandem sprint events, also winning a gold at the 2024 Paralympics in the tandem B kilo alongside his pilot Steffan Lloyd.

In 2022, he was Team Wales' first Commonwealth medallist and first gold medallist This time Ball delivered the first cycling podium position in the men's B tandem 1,000m time trial.

Ball and Rotherham matched the silver they won in Birmingham with great rival Neil Fachie from Scotland taking the gold.

It was a third successive Commonwealth Games second place in this event for Ball.

"It is special to equal to what we did in Birmingham four years ago," said Ball.

"We have to be proud of what we've done. We gave it everything on the track and I was on the floor for 20 minutes afterwards."

Fachie effectively came out of retirement for this event and now has six Commonwealth Games golds and one silver to his name.

The rivalry between Fachie and Ball is long-standing with Rotherham having been the pilot for both men.

Fachie won gold in this event four years ago, while the results were reversed in the tandem sprint.

So Ball and Rotherham will have a chance to defend their sprint title on Saturday.

Rotherham, who hails from Bolton, said: "I spent three days learning the Welsh national anthem and I'm gutted I didn't get to sing it today.

"Hopefully we will do on Saturday."

Not long after those exploits, Oliva celebrated coming out of retirement as part of the team pursuit bronze-medal winning squad.

Oliva, 36, rode with Megan Barker, Jessica Roberts and Anna Morris at her third Games and finished on the podium by beating England in the race for third place.

Wales had qualified third fastest in a time in the morning session and later defeated England's Josie Knight, Grace Lister, Madelaine Leech and Abigail Miller in the afternoon programme.

Oliva had initially finished competitive cycling after the 2018 Gold Coast games following a career where she won World and European Championship medals and was the unused Team GB rider at the 2016 Olympics in the squad that won gold.

After having her three children with her cycling husband Lewis, both riders decided to return to the track for the Glasgow game. The family were there to watch Mummy win a medal.

"It means everything, the whole comeback was worthwhile and it means so much to me and to my family," said Ciara.

"To be riding alongside these girls is the biggest honour, they're absolutely awesome, it's just amazing."

Oliva gave her husband a little kiss after her race while he was warming up on the bike for his chance at a podium position.

But it was not to be. Oliva was due to compete in the men's bronze medal sprint race, alongside Steffan Lloyd and Hepburn.

The men's trio could not compete because Hepburn was feeling ill. He initially made to the start line but pulled out after receiving medical advice.

Oliva and Lloyd were on the start line when the final decision was made, Trinidad and Tobago were awarded the bronze and Hepburn left the arena distraught.

It shows how cruel professional sport can be.

The men's team pursuit quartet of Rhys Britton, Rory Gravelle, William Roberts and William Salter might have also just failed to reach the podium after losing the bronze medal race against New Zealand.

But the Wales track cycling squad will mostly be delighted with the start of this Commonwealth campaign.

With more medals on the horizon in the next three days.

title: How a three-year-old helped Fachie become Scotland record-breaker
description: Neil Fachie was done with cycling. The Commonwealth Games was a farewell. On Thursday, it turned into so much more than that.
fullText:
All Neil Fachie wanted after hirpling off his bike at the side of the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome track was to find his three-year-old son in the crowd.

For the previous few minutes, as his heart burned, lungs roared and legs ached during four flat-out laps, the 42-year-old just kept repeating the little boy's name. "Fraser, Fraser, Fraser."

"The last two laps of the race, he was all I was thinking about," Fachie told BBC Sport Scotland. "He was the motivation. Just saying his name over and over while I was seeing stars and ready to collapse was what I needed."

The mantra kept the Aberdonian pumping and, ultimately, took him all the way to a sixth Commonwealth Games gold medal after first Australia, then favourites Wales, failed to better Scotland's time.

It was the nation's first cycling medal on the first day of the competition, and a second followed when the women's team sprint trio of Lauren Bell, Iona Moir and Maddy Silcock saw off the Australians in the bronze-medal race.

NHS physio Silcock led them off, before Moir took over. Then double world medallist Bell maintained the pace until the end to claim a podium place.

"It's one of those things you imagine when you're doing a hard session," Bell told BBC Sport Scotland. "You have nerves by you're just out there finding joy in riding for your nation. That takes the nerves off and luckily we've come away with bronze."

Glasgow 2026 'great way to go out', says Fachie

Fachie & Graham compete at 2026 Commonwealth Games

What are the different cycling events at Commonwealth Games?

No Scottish athlete has ever won more golds than Fachie.

Not Duncan Scott, who tells the spectators to 'haud yer wheesht' in a recorded message before every race here. Not Alex 'Tattie Marshall. Not even Hoy, who was cheering as hard as ever other Scot in the room.

Fachie knew where he stood. Knew the accolade he could claim.

But he did not think he was capable of achieving it here in the Tandem B 1,000m event. After all, he effectively retired after the Paris Paralympics two years ago.

Life since then has been spent with wife Lora and toddler Fraser, visiting a velodrome now and then and working 9-5 for Amazon. Training happens once a week when life allows or, more candidly, when he can be bothered.

"I had walked away from cycling," the four-time Paralympic medallist said. "If it hadn't been a home Games, I wouldn't be here. I thought 'let's go and say our farewells' but I genuinely didn't expect to win gold because I'm not training much."

And yet Fachie found himself standing on a podium in Glasgow on Thursday afternoon, lip quivering, and listening to Flower of Scotland.

Beside the diminutive dynamo was the hulking figure of English pilot Aaron Pope, who had never been on a tandem before this year.

"With the amount he's won, he would be fully entitled to be apprehensive but he jumped in straight at the deep end," Pope said. "On several occasions, we've almost binned it, and he just goes, 'Yeah, it's all right. Bad things happen'.

"He's obviously a good bike rider, but he's just a far better bloke. He's juggling his family, a full-time job, and he's still coming in every Wednesday - not overly happy necessarily all the time, but always giving me everything he can. So, in return, it's easy to put in the work for him."

Pope's other responsibility on Thursday was to help visually-impared Fachie find Lora and Fraser, once the old man had leapt off the bike and gambolled up the steep banking towards the crowd.

"I could have been wandering that stand for a while trying to find them," said the Scot, wryly. "Giving Fraser a big hug was was the best thing. I'm dying to go up and show him my medal soon as well."

Fachie will be back here on Saturday. He doesn't expect to win the tandem sprint, but he didn't expect to win the kilo either.

But what he does expect is that it will be the last race of a career that has delivered more than he ever imagined it might.

"I don't see any way I'm racing beyond Saturday," he said. "Things happen in life, but I'm walking away saying that's it, because there's no better way to go out than racing here in front of a home crowd. It is the end. There's no doubt."

title: Higgins 'big believer in Irish League summer football'
description: Coleraine manager Ruaidhri Higgins says "a worry for me is if we do not move to summer football, then it is never going to improve" after his side's 8-0 aggregate defeat by HJK Helsinki ended their Uefa Conference League qualifying hopes.
fullText:
Coleraine manager Ruaidhri Higgins said "a worry for me is if we do not move to summer football, then it is never going to improve" after his side's 8-0 aggregate defeat by HJK Helsinki ended their Uefa Conference League qualifying hopes.

HJK had a comfortable five-goal lead after the first leg and, at Inver Park, displayed more ruthlessness in front of goal to register a 3-0 win.

Coleraine are the third Irish Premiership team to bow out of the Conference League qualifiers after Linfield and Glentoran exited in the first round, with Larne the only Northern Irish side who still have a chance of securing a European group stage spot this season.

The Irish Premiership campaign currently takes place over the more traditional months of August to early May, but Higgins believes a switch to summer football would benefit the league.

"I've been a big believer in summer football," Higgins told BBC Sport NI after the game.

"I have to be honest, I think that to stop these kinds of results, to help our teams in Europe and we are potentially going to lose a European place, we have to change that.

"And how do you change it? You have to be more matched up and in better condition for this level of game going forward. There is a worry for me that if we don't move to summer football, then it's never ever going to improve. We need every advantage that we can get."

Clinical HJK end Coleraine's European hopes

Higgins previously managed League of Ireland side Derry City, whose European aspirations also came to an end on Thursday night after they lost against Croatia's Rijeka.

However, Shelbourne and Bohemians advanced to the third qualifying round with Higgins adding that League of Ireland has strengthened since moving to the summer football model.

The League of Ireland is played primarily over the summer months with their season running from mid-February to early November.

"I think 25 years ago the League of Ireland and the Irish League were on a level playing field and there was nothing between the two leagues," he continued.

"Since the League of Ireland has gone to summer football it's got better and nobody can argue that point. It's overtaken this league and results in Europe have proven it. I don't think that things are going to change if we don't change.

"People don't like change but what is best for the league is for me, in my opinion, that we go to summer football for a load of different reasons, European results being one of them."

Coleraine made a bright start to the second leg in Larne and had multiple half chances before HJK further extended their lead through Toivo Mero, Alfie Cicale and Mouhamed Gueye.

The Bannsiders were also denied by the post in the closing stages as they pushed to give the home fans something to cheer about before the full-time whistle.

"HJK are just elite attacking players and boys that are seasoned playing in Europe," Higgins added.

"The score definitely doesn't reflect the course of the 180 minutes, absolutely not. They've [HJK] even said that themselves.

"The score was very, very harsh on us. It was a lot closer than what it might suggest."

It has been a challenging few weeks for Coleraine after club captain Mark Coyle ruptured his anterior cruciate ligament [ACL] and Aidan Wilson also picked up an injury in Helsinki.

Higgins added that the side are now going to be without stopper Ryan Schofield and will need to bring more personnel in before the Irish Premiership season starts.

"We're having a few issues body-wise.

"Ryan Schofield has to have an operation in the next 24 hours. He had a training ground collision yesterday and that's another injury in that area of the pitch.

"We're having problems in the defensive side of the pitch in terms of injuries and stuff like that, so it's something that we need to sort out and we will."

title: Proud Keith wins bronze in front of 100-year-old grandad
description: Megan Keith claims a memorable Commonwealth Games bronze for Scotland in the 5000m in front of her 100-year-old grandad at Scotstoun Stadium.
fullText:
Megan Keith's grandad had two goals. To make it to 100 years old and then to watch the Commonwealth Games.

Dr Murray Kirkwood achieved both - and even saw his granddaughter win a bronze medal in the women's 5000m at Scotstoun.

He's no stranger to the ground. As an ardent Glasgow Warriors fan, he delivered the match ball before Franco Smith's side hosted Benetton in March, days before he became a centenarian.

He's had some memorable nights round these parts, but watching Megan tear to the podium should eclipse them. Well, so she hopes...

"He's a bit of a phenomenon," Keith, who finished a disappointing ninth in the 10,000m earlier in the week, told BBC Scotland.

"He worked hard to get here tonight, hopefully he's had the week of his life.

"He's proud of me whatever I do but I was so happy to put in a performance I can be proud of alongside him.

"When he delivered the match ball, he said that was the night of his life, so I was trying my best to rival that tonight... I'll have to go and ask him for his verdict!"

How a three-year-old helped Fachie become Scotland record-breaker

Evans battles nerves to become Scotland's breakout star

Kerr and Wightman revel in Wednesday warm-up for mile final

Given Keith herself was a tad surprised she scooped up a medal here, her grandad's take on the event ought to be a good one.

The 10,000m is her preference, but the longer distance final did not go to plan on Monday and she finished seventh.

The Inverness athlete said she was faced with the 'can Megan win a medal?' talk earlier this week, but with that weight of expectation lifted - combined with experience of the home crowd and "the help of two other Scots in the race" - she was freed from the shackles to soar to a classy and courageous run.

"If you look at Monday on paper, that was pretty disappointing," the 24-year-old added.

"I don't think you'd put me in the running for a 5km medal since the 10km is normally closer to being my strength, so that definitely helped, the removal of that pressure.

"I think I knew if I felt horrendous and dropped out or fell off the pace again it wouldn't really matter so I may as well shoot my shot."

And shoot she did. Biding her time in the middle of the congested pact, Keith made her move with four laps to go, weaving past early pacesetters from Kenya and Uganda.

She was afforded a bit of breathing space with two hurls around the track to go. But as expected, the exceptional Australian duo of Rose Davies - who made it a double gold at these Games with her 10km - and Jessica Hull, the 1500m Olympic silver medallist, entered another gear in the final lap.

While the cameras focused on the tremendous tussle between the pair in the matching yellow vests, the majority of the crowd had their eyes a wee bit further back, bawling at Keith on the final stretch.

She was home safe and sound. And swiftly searching for a saltire.

Once that was draped over her shoulders, and she'd caught up with fellow Scots Eloise Walker and Laura Muir, who finished 15th and 16th respectively, she was darting back around the track - the wrong way, this time - in search of her grandad.

He was eventually found for a quick hug, but a bigger debrief - and the declaration, surely, that this topped any other Scotstoun occasion - is still to be had.

title: Hull responds to criticism of prank on caddie
description: Golfer Charley Hull tells critics to "lighten up" after receiving backlash for a scratchcard prank she played on her caddie.
fullText:
Golfer Charley Hull has told critics to "lighten up" after receiving backlash for a scratchcard prank she played on her caddie.

In the lead up to the ongoing Women's Open at Royal Lytham & St Annes, Hull revealed she had purchased the ticket in a Blackpool joke shop and used it to trick caddie Adam Woodward into believing he had won £100,000 – a moment she caught on camera.

While many people have seen the funny side of the incident, Hull has faced criticism both on social media and from figures within golf, including four-time major winner Dame Laura Davies, who described the stunt as "extremely cruel" when asked about it on commentary.

However, Hull has refused to apologise for her actions, with the 30-year-old stating she would "100%" do it again.

Thitikul leads Open as Ryu and Kuwaki chase

"People that have complaints about it, I would say loosen up," said Hull.

"I don't have my social media on my phone on tournament weeks. I delete it and when I go home I'll add it again. I don't really like people seeing me and tagging me and stuff. I like to keep in the present moment.

"But I think people need to lighten up if they're taking that too seriously because it was pretty funny."

On Woodward, she added: "He thought it was funny after, he is not uptight. It's a joke. If people don't like it they can lump it, do you know what I mean?

"I felt bad for Adam but at the end of the day I have just got to have a good week. At the end of the week I'll buy him 100 scratchcards."

title: Brave move off foot of table with win over Phoenix
description: Wickets from three consecutive deliveries help Southern Brave close out a first win of the season in The Hundred, beating Birmingham Phoenix by 12 runs.
fullText:
The Hundred men's competition, Utilita Bowl

Southern Brave 128-8 (100 balls): Stoinis 34 (26); Rehan 3-25

Birmingham Phoenix 116-9 (100 balls): Smeed 35 (28); Wood 3-24

Wickets from three consecutive deliveries helped Southern Brave close out a first win of the season in The Hundred, beating Birmingham Phoenix by 12 runs at the Utilita Bowl.

With Phoenix needing 14 to win, Luke Wood had Ben Dwarshuis and Scott Currie caught off the first two balls of the final set.

Saqib Mahmood was then run out by Adil Rashid's direct hit and Brave conceded just one single off the next two balls as Phoenix closed on 116-9, well short of their target of 129.

Will Smeed top-scored for Phoenix, reaching 35 before he became Wood's first victim, the left-arm seamer finishing with figures of 3-24.

Marcus Stoinis took 2-16, removing Joe Clarke and Laurie Evans, while the England duo of Rashid (1-18) and Jofra Archer (1-21) kept it tight.

Having been put into bat, Brave lost Jamie Smith, caught by Mitch Owen off Dwarshuis, after seven balls of their innings.

They failed to put on a partnership greater than 33, with Ben McKinney (18), Tom Abell (22), Stoinis (34) and David Miller (24) all chipping in before getting out, while Rehan Ahmed was the pick of the Phoenix bowlers with 3-25.

Brave lost four middle-order wickets for 12 runs as the innings moved towards its conclusion, before a five-ball 10 from Wood, batting at number 10, helped them to a winning score of 128-8.

The win allows Brave to leapfrog Phoenix and rise off the bottom of the table, moving into seventh on net run-rate.

title: England edge South Africa thriller to reach semis
description: England's netballers reach the Commonwealth Games semi-finals after producing a pulsating comeback to beat South Africa 58-54.
fullText:
England's netballers reached the Commonwealth Games semi-finals after producing a pulsating comeback to beat South Africa 58-54.

With both sides tied on six points but the Roses ahead of the Proteas on goal average in pool A's second spot going into the game, England had to avoid defeat to progress.

Elmere van der Berg was in fine form early on to fire South Africa into a six-goal lead at the end of the first quarter with 16 of her nation's 17 goals, leaving England facing an uphill task.

But some excellent and aggressive defensive work by second-quarter substitute Halimat Adio helped England spring multiple counter-attacks to claw their way back to just 29-28 down at the halfway stage.

The Roses started to take control in the third quarter, opening up a seven-goal lead at one stage before the Proteas netted three times in quick succession to go into the final 15 minutes 43-39 behind.

Both sides then went blow for blow in a compelling final quarter with 15 goals apiece, but 2018 champions England held on to ensure they maintained their record of qualifying for every Commonwealth Games semi-final since the inaugural netball event in 1998.

England will face New Zealand in the last four on Saturday, while South Africa's wait for a first semi-final since 1998 goes on.

Commonwealth Games netball final pool standings, external

England captain Fran Williams was full of praise for her whole team after Olivia Tchine scored 41 goals and Lois Pearson netted 17 times, but she picked out goalkeeper Adio in particular for her remarkable display from the bench.

"I feel like she was unreal for us from that second quarter," Williams told TNT Sports.

"So proud of her, bringing that energy to get us back in the game when we needed it."

The 28-year-old said there was "no denying" England have been under pressure all week to perform and challenge for a medal.

"So for us to be able to finish out a game like that, riding the wave of goal for goal and to come out on top, just so proud of the team," Williams added.

"We don't shy away from [pressure]. We are the first people to put the pressure on ourselves because we know what we are capable of in our own environment.

"We've got so many young heads out there that are showing experience way beyond their years. I just want to try and be that rock for them and let the others shine around me."

It is perhaps no surprise that the four highest ranking nations in the world have reached the semi-final.

Australia - the world number one, four-time Commonwealth Games winners and reigning champions - are undoubtedly the team to beat once again in 2026.

They will face Jamaica on Saturday, who have never won gold in the competition but came agonisingly close in the 2022 final when they were beaten 55-51 by the Diamonds.

The number four ranked Sunshine Girls have won bronze on three occasions.

Two-time winners and world number two side New Zealand beat England, who are currently ranked third, in the bronze medal match at the last Games but have not won gold since claiming back-to-back titles in 2006 and 2010.

title: Is Infantino finished? Could Uefa boycott World Cup? What happens now?
description: It's been a seismic 48 hours for football after Uefa threatened to boycott the World Cup and Concacaf rejected Gianni Infantino's funding plan - what happens now, and can Fifa's president survive?
fullText:
The bombshell statement landed at 16:00 BST on Thursday, 30 July.

In terms of impact, European football's governing body Uefa could not have gone any bigger.

"Uefa and its national associations will not participate in Fifa competitions," it said.

Eleven brutal words. The definitive reaction to Fifa president Gianni Infantino's plan to sell a 20% stake in a subsidiary company set up to run the world governing body's competitions, including the World Cup.

A company it is intended Fifa will run but that will be part-funded by private investors, including the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Joshua Kushner.

It feels as though no-one who matters knows how this situation is going to play out just yet.

"Not sure the detail was considered when deciding the overall policy," was the response from a senior European football source when asked what this decision means for the U20 Women's World Cup, starting on 5 September, being hosted by Poland and featuring plenty of European nations.

Uefa's boycott threat will be activated if Infantino's funding deal is accepted.

Given 19 September is the deadline for countries to accept Fifa's deal and bank $20m (£15m) on 1 January, in theory, countries could be pulling out of that tournament in the middle of the quarter-finals and before the semis.

After that, the next senior matches in a Fifa competition are the Women's World Cup play-offs in October, which feature England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland among others.

"Wales is involved in the play-offs for the Women's World Cup in the autumn, and it would be our first qualification for a World Cup," Uefa vice-president and ex-Wales international Laura McAllister told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Nobody can even countenance the thought of not being involved in those.

"But let's be clear here. This is not a problem of Uefa's making. It's a problem that Fifa have created. Nobody wants the players to suffer, and nobody wants nations to suffer when it comes to the most prestigious competitions.

"We've been pushed into this corner and that's Fifa's responsibility."

Uefa to boycott World Cups if Fifa plans approved

Is World Cup sell-off plan a step too far by Infantino?

Uefa threatens full Fifa boycott over World Cup sale plans

No-one can be certain what happens now. And no-one knows what the future for Infantino is.

Fifa is yet to respond to Uefa's statement, which was followed up by another from Concacaf, which governs football in North and Central America and hosted this year's World Cup, saying their 41 members rejected the proposals.

Yet, in a sense, it is not Fifa's argument.

Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt is a Fifa vice-president. She spoke out against the plan at Uefa's emergency meeting on Thursday. The FA said it stands "shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues" on the matter.

Scottish FA president Mike Mulraney is also chair of Fifa's finance committee. The Scottish FA's statement said the organisation "agrees unequivocally" with Uefa's stance.

The repeated responses from those who have spoken out are of fury at the lack of proper consultation and lack of dialogue from Infantino, including with his Fifa colleagues, as much as with the proposals themselves.

"Anger," said one source, when asked for the prevailing mood at Uefa's emergency meeting.

Infantino became Fifa president in 2016 when he beat Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88. The Swiss is due to stand for a fourth term in March.

Prior to this week, it had been anticipated he would be re-elected unopposed. FAs around the world, including some in Europe, have already confirmed their intention to support the 56-year-old.

But sources say in addition to rejecting Infantino's plan, the vast majority of the Concacaf members are either losing faith in the Fifa president's ability to govern the game, or have lost it altogether.

Now there is talk of trying to find someone to stand against him.

The name of Nasser Al-Khelaifi has been mentioned. This is understandable. Qatari Al-Khelaifi is already one of the most powerful figures in football, not only through his status as president of back-to-back Champions League winners Paris St-Germain but his leadership of European clubs.

Previously known as the European Clubs' Association, Al-Khelaifi took over as chairman in the aftermath of the other seismic event that threatened to pull the game apart - the ill-fated European Super League, which collapsed within 48 hours in 2021.

Al-Khelaifi presided over a name change - to European Football Clubs. More importantly, he expanded it to over 800 members. Of the biggest clubs, only Real Madrid remain outside.

In theory, he would be the best person to challenge Infantino. But he doesn't want to. "He genuinely, genuinely, genuinely doesn't want the job," was the response of a source close to the 52-year-old when asked about the possibility on Thursday.

Historically, sitting Fifa presidents are not challenged in elections. The last president to lose an election was Englishman Sir Stanley Rous when he was beaten by Brazilian Joao Havelange in 1974.

"I don't know, in all honesty," said McAllister, when asked if Infantino will keep his job.

Former FA chairman David Bernstein was asked the same question by BBC Sport.

"In a normal organisation, if he has to back down due to something of this magnitude he'd probably be shown the door," Bernstein said.

"But Fifa is not a normal organisation. If he has the support of enough of the national associations, he will continue."

Former Uefa chief executive Lars-Christer Olsson told the BBC that Infantino has overplayed his hand and his position could be in trouble.

He suggested Fifa should instigate a reform where the presidency circulates around figures from different confederations "rather than giving people so much power" as it has done with Infantino and his predecessors, Switzerland's Sepp Blatter and Brazil's Havelange.

When asked if Infantino should be removed from his role, Olsson said: "I think that should be a new start for football."

Fifa offers $40m if nations back controversial plan

Courting controversy and befriending Trump - Fifa's 'unlikely saviour'

Uefa and PM criticise Infantino World Cup plan

While Uefa only covers 55 of Fifa's 211 national associations, in pure playing terms, it is the most powerful confederation by far.

In the last edition of the World Cup, the Women's World Cup and the Club World Cup - Fifa's flagship events - Uefa supplied three of the four semi-finalists.

If there was no European involvement in a Fifa competition, the commercial impact would be seismic and ensure there was virtually no chance of Infantino hitting the figures he has promised in a letter to the national associations, when he talked about a $40bn (£30bn) product.

David Bernstein feels a solution has to be found.

"I can't believe in the long term that there will be a schism because it would be a lose-lose for everybody," he said.

"Fifa can't afford not to have European nations play in their competitions and frankly Europe can't afford not to be part of it.

"On this occasion, Infantino's got to back down. This deal is not acceptable. It's a friends deal and it's not right. If they want to raise capital, there's other, better ways of doing it."

McAllister accuses Fifa of 'blackmail' over World Cup plan

title: Vomit in the morning, gold in the afternoon for England's gamblers
description: Sickness struck England's team pursuit squad on Thursday morning, but a late gamble and fine ride secured Commonwealth Games gold in the velodrome.
fullText:
"At the end of the day it's just riding around in circles."

Will Tidball is being modest. England's team pursuit win at the Commonwealth Games was far from straightforward.

Earlier in the day, after a ragged qualifying run, world champion Josh Charlton threw up over his team-mate's bike.

It meant a late change in the line-up - to one they had never run before. Still they beat Olympic champions Australia to gold.

"I wasn't actually meant to be doing this event this evening," Tidball told BBC Sport.

"To get subbed in, having not done any efforts in this team, or in this track, or in this order, it was always going to be a bit of a gamble."

How a three-year-old helped Fachie become Scotland record-breaker

England's Campbell retains Commonwealth weightlifting title

The first signs of trouble came in the morning qualifying.

In the team pursuit, riders start as a quartet before dropping to three when the one at the front has given everything.

Those final three are supposed to cross the line together but Charlton, the world champion from the individual event, became detached with four laps to go and was still emerging from the final bend when team-mates Charlie Tanfield and Ethan Vernon crossed the line ahead.

Changes in personnel for finals are not uncommon in team pursuiting. In fact, the opposite is true.

But switching to an untested team is a gamble.

England had been two seconds adrift of Australia in qualifying. Something had to be done.

"There is strategy in play, different heights and orders," said Tanfield, the veteran of this team at 29.

"Me and Ethan finished ahead of them [Australia's qualifying time].

"We knew if we had a clean ride we could beat them.

"I just kept reminding the lads - even if you are behind things can change."

The changes meant Tidball, Tanfield and Vernon lined up alongside 19-year-old Henry Hobbs, who is competing at his first major championships.

"You have just got to go through your own process," Vernon said.

"It didn't change what I had to do. I had the same role, same turn lengths and went through my own rhythm."

Even in the final, momentum swung. England built an early lead before Australia crept their way back to have the advantage shortly after halfway.

But, crucially, Hobbs clung on - England staying as a quartet for three punishing laps after Australia had dropped to a trio.

Every extra turn helps those shielded behind him, leaving 

"Henry did way longer than he should have done on the front and so did Charlie," Vernon said.

"I could tell we were up [ahead of Australia] but we were also starting to fall apart a bit.

"I was glancing across the track and trying to do enough to not drop my team-mate but also stay ahead of the Aussies."

Gaps began to appear between English wheels as the noise in the crowd grew louder.

Vernon and Tanfield were part of the Team GB quartet beaten by Australia in the Paris Olympics final. Spare a thought for Charlton watching on, helpless.

"It was more nerve-wracking than being in it," he said.

"It was tight at times but I had faith they were going to pull away at the end and they did."

In the end, England won by 1.131 seconds. Their time of three minutes 47.092 seconds was a new Commonwealth Games record and the Australians had been dethroned.

As ever in track cycling, there is a race on and off the track.

This was a marker from England for the rest of this event and the Olympics in two years' time, when Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland can add reinforcements too.

"The Aussies always turn up to Commonwealth Games," Vernon said.

"They go full equipment, good skinsuit, good equipment, everything.

"In England we go with a different mindset. We save stuff for the Olympics.

"We don't have the best skinsuits. We are doing the best we can and to beat them without that is special."

For Tanfield this was a second Commonwealth gold, eight years after his first in the individual event.

Vernon added this gold to others in the national, European and World Championships. For him, only the Olympics remains.

Charlton, who hopes to be fit for the individual event on Friday, and Tidball now have their first Commonwealth medals to add to others won on the world stage.

"I wasn't quite on the money today but we will see how it goes tomorrow," Charlton said. "I will give it everything I have got in me."

But the moment was, perhaps, most special for teenager Hobbs.

"It is my first year as an elite. Even getting selected for this was a big surprise," he said.

"To pull off the win is amazing."

There is far more to it than riding in circles.

title: Thitikul leads Open as Ryu and Kuwaki chase
description: World number two Jeeno Thitikul leads the first round of the AIG Women's Open by two shots after a spectacular seven-under 64 at Royal Lytham & St Anne's.
fullText:
-7 A Thitikul (Tha); -5 S Kuwaki (Jpn), H Ryu (Kor); -4 Y Noh (US), C Boutier (Fra); -3 C Iwai (Jpn), C Wannasaen (Tha); -2 P Martin (Esp), L Coughlin (US), C Hull (Eng), R Takeda (Jpn), M Saigo (Jpn), L Woad (Eng), S Tan (Sin).

Selected others: -1 A Hewson (Eng), E Rhodes (Eng), A Fuller (Eng), L Ko (NZ), +1 M Yamashita (Jpn), +2 N Korda.

World number two Jeeno Thitikul leads the first round of the AIG Women's Open by two shots after a spectacular seven-under 64 at Royal Lytham & St Anne's.

The 23-year-old has 11 top-10 finishes in majors but has never won one, and went bogey-free in a fine start to her latest attempt.

South Korea's Haeran Ryu, aiming to become only the fifth woman in history to claim three majors in a calendar year, is second alongside Japan's Shiho Kuwaki on five under.

England's Lottie Woad and Charley Hull are both on two under, while compatriot Alice Hewson led the tournament in the morning and finished one under.

"Winning one [major] doesn't mean I am going to have a really good, successful career," Thitikul said.

"Winning one doesn't mean much, I would rather be a consistent player, more than just winning one and then gone.

"Sometimes I had a hard time dealing with all the noise."

The world's best golfers performed well in the opening round, with world number one Nelly Korda one of the few stars to fall behind.

Korda remains off the pace after shooting a two-over-par 73 in a round that included four bogeys.

Hull responds to criticism of prank on caddie

Korda & Hull seek major glory - Women's Open tee times

Thailand's Thitikul, who was leapfrogged by Korda as world number one when she won the Chevron Championship in April, sunk seven birdies in a faultless round.

Her round included three straight birdies on the front nine and difficult par saves.

Earlier this month, Ryu, 25, claimed her second major in the space of two weeks at the Evian Championship.

That form continued as four birdies on the front nine quickly took her to the top of the leaderboard.

Despite a bogey on the 15th, Ryu finished with two birdies in the last three holes.

Last year's Open champion Miyu Yamashita shot one-over-par, while three-time major winner Lydia Ko is even par.

Royal Lytham & St Anne's has hosted the Women's Open twice and had British winners both times - Scotland's Catriona Matthew in 2009 and England's Georgia Hall in 2018 - and the class of 2026 are aiming to keep that run going.

Woad, 22, finished tied for seventh at this year's Chevron Championship, backing up top-10 finishes at last year's Open and Evian Championship.

Having coming in as one of the favourites, her bogey-free round of 69 leaves her well poised after day one.

"Good start. No bogeys, which is always a good round here. Hit a lot of fairways and a lot of greens. Didn't make too many putts," she said.

Hull, a five-time runner up in majors, had yet another near-miss in June's US Open and will be hoping to finally get over the line.

Four birdies on the front nine gave the 30-year-old an ideal start as she aims to go one better than her runner-up finishes in 2023 and 2025.

Despite sinking six birdies, four bogeys pegged back Hull, who showed great skill to save par from the bunker on the 18th.

"I was super nervous on the first tee. I was so nervous. It's even more nerve-wracking when you're having to hit an iron because you have to stripe an iron shot," Hull said.

"I missed quite a few putts today that I felt I should have holed, but I felt like I stayed in there pretty well considering how nervous I was, because I feel there was a lot of pressure on me out there."

Hall, the most recent British female player to win a major, is back playing after giving birth five months ago.

The 30-year-old endured a tough opening round to end the day five over.

Korda started the year with two major titles, and any talk of a career Grand Slam seemed ambitious, even by her own high standards.

However, as the LPGA recognises a player as having achieved the career Grand Slam by winning four of the five major titles, Korda's victory at the US Open in June has given her a chance to enter the history books.

The 28-year-old, playing alongside Ryu, got off to a slow start with bogeys on the second and third holes but recovered those shots to reach the back nine at even par.

From hoping for a career Grand Slam, Korda will now have to fight to make Friday's cut.
